#6718. Safe Word: The Best Jewelry Launches of November 2026

Safe Word is a series highlighting the latest trends in the jewelry market, keeping you up to date on all things that sparkle and shine.

November’s jewelry launches are looking both backward and forward, with designers revisiting their roots, reworking archival ideas, and stepping into entirely new territory. First up, Pomellato reaches back to 1997 to revive “Moneta Orientale” as a colorful modern talisman; David Yurman celebrates the magic of a New York holiday with Michael B. Jordan, Yerin Ha, and Inde Navarrette; Vhernier revisits its iconic “Trottola” design with new proportions and contrasting materials; Di Volpe reimagines the classic tennis bracelet with customizable gemstones in “DiSegno”; and Brent Neale transforms the classic bow into sculptural fine jewelry with “Wrap It Up.”

Elsewhere, Grace Winfrey looks to Italian good-luck charms for the colorful “Poppy Fortuna”; Robinson Pelham checks into “Suite 96” to celebrate 30 years of bold jewelry; Le Vian brings Georgian-era romance to Jared with a new collection of warm-toned diamonds; and Wempe puts traditional goldsmithing at the center of “au:thentic,” inspired by the humble jump ring. From archival revivals and meaningful motifs to innovative designs and new creative directions, November’s launches prove that sometimes the best way forward starts with looking back.

For the rest of the month, we’ve got you covered on all the jewelry-related happenings worth knowing about.

Pomellato is looking to its archives for its latest good-luck charm. For the newest chapter of “Memorie d’Archivio,” the maison revives Moneta Orientale, a 1997 pendant inspired by the ancient symbolism of a circle surrounding a square, representing the harmony between heaven and earth. Reimagined for today in 33 stone-and-pavé combinations, the design pairs colorful hard stones including black jade, amazonite, sodalite, rhodochrosite, and labradorite with Pomellato’s signature irregular pavé of diamonds, sapphires, rubies, and more. Offered in two proportions, each pendant transforms the archival motif into a modern talisman for prosperity and protection.

David Yurman Captures the Magic of a New York Holiday

David Yurman is celebrating the magic of the holidays in New York City with a new campaign featuring global brand ambassador Michael B. Jordan alongside actresses Yerin Ha and Inde Navarrette. Set against a snow-covered Washington Square Park, the campaign captures a series of quintessential New York moments, from Jordan and Ha facing off in a spirited card game to Navarrette hailing a cab in search of the perfect holiday gift. Throughout the campaign, the cast wears some of the house’s most recognizable designs, including 18-karat gold Cable bracelets and pieces from the “Starburst” and “Armory” collections. Directed by Bradford Young and photographed by Drew Vickers, the campaign brings together the spirit of the city, the joy of togetherness, and the timeless appeal of David Yurman’s jewelry.

Vhernier’s ‘Trottola’ Takes on a New Form

Vhernier is revisiting one of its most recognizable designs with a new interpretation of “Trottola,” the sculptural collection originally introduced in 2003. Inspired by the continuous motion of a spinning top, the latest designs play with proportions, contrasting materials, and asymmetrical shapes across rings, bracelets, necklaces, and earrings. Polished rose gold meets glossy black jet, with select pieces featuring diamond pavé for an added contrast of light and dark. The collection also focuses on versatility, from rings designed for stacking to convertible earclips that can be worn as studs or dangling earrings. With its fluid forms and unexpected material combinations, “Trottola” brings a fresh perspective to Vhernier’s signature sculptural approach to jewelry.

Di Volpe is rethinking the classic tennis bracelet with “DiSegno,” a new customizable fine jewelry system designed to change with its wearer. Using concealed, patent-pending connections, individual cultured diamonds and gemstones, called Elements, can be removed, rearranged, or added by hand, allowing wearers to transform bracelets into necklaces or earrings without compromising the seamless look of traditional tennis jewelry. The collection launches with 28 stone-and-cut combinations, including rubies, emeralds, sapphires, and diamonds, alongside a limited-edition collaboration with Lebanese artist Ali Cha’aban featuring five sculptural designs. With new cuts, colors, and artist collaborations planned for future releases, “DiSegno” makes the case for fine jewelry that’s never quite finished.

Brent Neale Reimagines the Bow in Fine Jewelry

Brent Neale is putting a bow on the holiday season with “Wrap It Up,” a new fine jewelry collection that transforms the familiar ribbon motif into sculptural works of art. Drawing inspiration from Old Hollywood glamour and the femininity of the 1960s, the designer plays with the contrast between rigid precious metals and the soft movement of fabric, crafting bows that twist, curl, and unfurl in 18-karat gold and platinum. Colored gemstones sit nestled within the ribbon-like forms, while pavé diamonds accentuate every curve and fold. Equal parts playful and precious, the collection brings a little gift-wrapped glamour to the jewelry box.

Grace Winfrey’s Latest Collection Is All About Good Fortune

Grace Winfrey is bringing a little extra luck to the jewelry box with “Poppy Fortuna,” a new fine jewelry collection inspired by the natural beauty of the Italian landscape and symbols of good fortune. Scarlet poppies, sunflowers, bees, four-leaf clovers, horseshoes, and ladybugs come to life through vibrant gemstones and intricate pavé, creating miniature mosaics of color and texture. Highlights include a Lucky Bangle combining three good-luck charms, sculptural sunflower earrings with tiny ladybugs tucked into their petals, and layered charm necklaces designed to feel like modern keepsakes. Handcrafted in New York City, each piece transforms familiar symbols of prosperity, protection, and happiness into playful, colorful works of art.

Robinson Pelham Channels ’90s Glamour for Its Anniversary

Robinson Pelham is closing out its 30th anniversary celebrations with “Suite 96,” a new campaign and collection launch inspired by the glamour of late-’90s London. Set inside a private suite at St. James’s Hotel & Club in Mayfair, the campaign reimagines jewelry as the ultimate room service, with diamonds arriving on trays, gold spilling out of wardrobes, and plenty of pieces to layer before a night out. At the center is “Studio 30,” a four-piece anniversary collection featuring diamond necklaces and statement earrings, including the sculptural Via and Hira necklaces, cascading diamond drops, and the bold Solstice Supreme. Alongside the anniversary designs, the house introduces new collections and additions to existing favorites, from chunky gold links and graphic heart rings to colorful enamel and gemstone combinations. Together, the launches celebrate three decades of Robinson Pelham’s bold, playful approach to fine jewelry.

Le Vian and Jared Revive Georgian-Era Romance

Le Vian is bringing a little old-world romance to Jared Jewelers with its new exclusive “Georgian Chocolate & Nude Diamonds” collection. Inspired by the candlelit jewels of the Georgian era, when jewelry was designed to capture and reflect the warmth of natural light, the collection reimagines historic buttercup settings in polished Honey Gold, with eight rounded prongs framing each natural diamond. The designs pair Le Vian’s signature Chocolate and Nude Diamonds with warm gold detailing across solitaire rings, anniversary bands, tennis bracelets, necklaces, and earrings. Select styles introduce colorful gemstones including Chocolate Quartz, Green Apple Peridot, and Grape Amethyst, giving the vintage-inspired silhouettes a contemporary update. With its sculptural settings and warm-toned stones, the collection brings the romance of antique jewelry into the present.

Wempe’s ‘Au:thentic’ Celebrates the Art of Goldsmithing

Wempe’s new gender-inclusive fine jewelry collection, “Au:thentic,” puts craftsmanship front and center, finding inspiration in the foundational skills taught to aspiring goldsmiths. The collection takes its shape from the jump ring, one of the first techniques Patrick Sieroslawski learned as an apprentice more than 22 years ago, translating its form to necklaces, bracelets, rings, earrings, and pendants. Handcrafted at Wempe’s atelier in Germany, the pieces come in 18-karat yellow, white, and rose gold, with select styles set with diamonds. “Au:thentic” also marks the beginning of a multiyear rollout, with three additional chapters set to expand on its design language through twists, wraps, and interlocking links.

#6716. Chris Rock on Directing an A24 Movie and ‘Crying Like a Bitch’ in Therapy

Chris Rock enters a room a bit diffidently, like he’s feeling out what’s inside, making quiet observations about the world around him that sometimes tip over into jokes and sometimes don’t. Because today we’re meeting on the 24th floor of the World Trade Center, I will not repeat the jokes. He looks around at the setup for the interview, which is being filmed: lights and cameras and microphones everywhere. “I just shot a movie with, like, three people,” he says. “It was much lower-budget than this.”

That movie is Misty Green, Rock’s fourth feature as a director. It’s about an actress named Misty, played by Rosalind Eleazar, who has talent and who has had success but who cannot quite get out of her own way. Rock identifies and he doesn’t. “I like to say there’s a part of me that’s been every character in the movie,” he says—including Misty’s best friend, played by Anna Kendrick, who is mostly there to crack jokes and report on her own unsatisfying romantic life. The film is a portrait of Hollywood that is dystopian but not cliché; Misty goes through hell, much of it of her own making, but her talent never dims. It has a lived, almost casual quality that belies Rock’s grasp of his craft: At 61, he hasn’t lost his eye for the telling, damning detail or hypocrisy, but there is also a warmth here, a genuine love for his characters. With Misty Green, you can feel both Rock’s lifetime of experience making things for audiences, and also something new—and more finely observed emerging.

All clothing, tie, and sunglasses by Tom Ford. Pocket square by Charvet.

Misty Green is part of a growing tradition in Rock’s work, including the previous film he directed, 2014’s Top Five, about the highs and lows of show business—something Rock has also chronicled, in exacting autobiographical detail, in his past two comedy specials: 2018’s Tamborine (which is about, among other things, Rock’s divorce) and 2023’s Selective Outrage (about, among other things, his encounter with Will Smith at the 2022 Academy Awards ceremony).

Rock has been at times the most famous man in all of comedy. His 1996 special Bring the Pain was a cultural phenomenon on a level few humans will ever experience. But as a director, he has increasingly been drawn to smaller ’70s-style character studies of people making an earnest attempt just to figure out themselves and their demons. “I’d love to make Man on Fire or something,” he says. “It’s not really my thing. I make a tailored suit. My suits are made by hand, by one guy. And it’s okay.”

This interview has been condensed and edited; watch this cover story—an episode of GQ’s One More Question—above or on YouTube, and listen on Spotify or Apple Podcasts.

Chris Rock: No, no. We’re going to be good. I think.

“How’d you get started?” “Were you funny in school?” Stuff like that. Whatever. I get it. You guys have a job. I’m not Harry Styles. Sometimes it requires a reintroduction.

I mean, it’s a thing you worry about every day. Am I still funny? Well—you don’t worry about being funny. You worry about being professionally funny. On a world-class level. I always had a joke: If I ever did a talk show, I’d do a morning show. I wouldn’t do a late-night show. Because I would only have to be funnier than Al Roker. You know what I mean? Al’s lovely, but I think I could take him in a joke-off.

You guys have a job, and the job is to get clickbait and things you can turn into controversy, and what’s the headline that has nothing to do with the actual article.

I mean, it’s your job, though. You might have better intentions, and I appreciate your interest. But a lot of what I read, it’s like: “Oh okay.” People want to talk about your personal life. I get it. We’re in a gossipy culture. We live in a world where Andy Cohen is Norman Lear and Ryan Murphy is Steven Spielberg. That is the world we live in. So people want gossip. We’re righteous people that follow nine commandments. And the one commandment we don’t follow is Thou shall not spread false witness. We are all about spreading false witness now. That is the world we live in. And that’s what journalism, or at least entertainment journalism, has become. Not that everything’s false, but it is definitely amplified to create sides, no matter what the issue is. How’s that? How am I doing?

Some of it is I got divorced. Nobody has a successful divorce, so that takes time. Then once it’s done, okay, you’re not sitting on the money you had before, so now you got to really make some money. So you go on tour, or two tours. So there was a lot of stand-up. There was a lot of getting my life together. You got a pandemic, you got a bunch of nonsense going on there.

I was not a great husband. I watched a lot of porn. I don’t watch porn anymore. I haven’t watched porn in five, six years.

It’s not anything I’m proud of, but it’s something I had to go through. It’s like you watch a Marvel movie, and the guy, he has to test his powers. You know what I mean? Every Marvel movie, man or woman, they have to test their powers. They’re assholes. They get these powers and they’re assholes, and they’re racing trains and they’re lifting up ocean liners and they try to go to the sun, then they crash down because they realize they’re not God. And then they start helping people. I tested my powers. I definitely realized I wasn’t God or anywhere near him, and I was severely humbled, as I should have been.

It’s basically Bring the Pain to Kill the Messenger. That’s one guy. Tamborine’s the beginning of a new guy. And that guy’s in fucking pain in Tamborine. That guy is damn near—Tamborine’s like the blues, man. Where Selective Outrage is like—there’s some pain in that one. Well, there’s a lot of pain in that one, but Tamborine is like: What have I become? [Starts singing Johnny Cash’s cover of Nine Inch Nails’ “Hurt.”] Goes away, in the end. I’m Johnny Cash with Rick Rubin, singing about my empire of dirt. That’s Tamborine. Tamborine is the fucking blues.

Yeah. I’m not one for a hint. You got to tell me exactly what the fuck you want. You have to tell me exactly what the fuck you mean.

A friend just kind of blurted it one day. You ever have somebody say something and you’re like, “Okay, let me get this looked into”? And it’s before Tamborine, but around that time. So I’m already quitting porn. You know what I mean? I’m already in a place where, “Okay, what the fuck’s wrong with me?” And I got a cognitive assessment test. And it’s like eight hours of testing to basically see—it’s the kind of thing you would get if you were bipolar or something. So it’s a lot of testing, and that’s what they came up with.

It made me realize how insensitive a lot of my behavior was throughout the years. Because it’s weird. I’ve got a friend who always says, this is a side joke, but he says, “When a schizophrenic sees a famous person, they go, ‘Ha, see? Told you!’ ” Mental illness and celebrity—it’s a weird combination there, because you think people are reacting a certain way because of celebrity. Because it’s this weird thing that you can’t quantify. So I used to just blame everything on celebrity. It’s like, “Oh, we’re not connecting because I had a chronic unique-ism.” I thought I was so fucking unique.

But also, okay, what are the symptoms? Black-and-white thinking. It’s an advantageous thing to have if you’re a comedian, black and white. Catastrophizing, great. You know what I mean? When you see one of those specials—okay, the average comedian, or even above average, probably does 40 shows before they record a special. And maybe they did 20 club things before this, so that’s 60 times onstage. My average special, I’ve gone onstage over 250 times. So I’m working it. It looks like I’m just, “Oh my God, he’s got this great insight.” But it’s like, “Yo man, I’m grinding this stuff.” Also, I have a hard time picking up on social cues, but I have a weirdly accurate ear. I can pick up on things in my ear. Sometimes I can pick up on a cue, but I can’t decipher it. I don’t know what just happened for a week, and I’m like, “Oh, that’s what she meant. Oh, that’s what he was trying to say.” It’s like my mind is working on the case. It just can’t solve it at that moment. Does that make sense?

Well, yeah. We do have this thing where everybody’s like—they brag about their therapy. Put it this way, my personal life wasn’t what I wanted it to be. And I’ll leave it at that. And that’s my relationship with everybody. So yeah, I went in there crying like a bitch. Like: What the fuck is going on?

You never come out. It’s an ongoing thing. You know what I mean? You’re always an alcoholic. So it’s a combination of therapy and what I have, NVLD, nonverbal learning disorder. So I have a person that helps me with that, and I have another therapist. I mean, it’s okay.

I mean, it’s not like a threat or anything. I’m just saying it’s okay. Whatever happened happened. Everybody saw it. I don’t really like talking about it. By the way—any awards show.

Yeah. Something happened. It wasn’t cool. And I would like to move on. I would like to—I had a nice career before it, and I know there’s a part of that that’s going to follow me the rest of my life. I got jokes. I got scripts. I got movie scripts. I got TV shows. I’m writing a book. I’m doing shit. I have a plethora of art I’m trying to get out, and that’s what I want you to pay attention to, not some crazy night.

I don’t get a lot of stuff. I honestly don’t. I mean, I probably get more offers as a director, to tell you the truth, than as an actor. It’s weird. When you’re really famous, it works for you and it works against you. So you got name recognition, but you also have people thinking they know what you can do and thinking that there’s a ceiling on your talent. So you got to fight that. The hardest thing you can do in show business is change perception. Reinvention is the hardest thing. So it’s kind of relatively easy to get famous, in the sense that it’s twice as hard to become a new person that is already famous. You know what I mean? The John Travolta that was on Welcome Back, Kotter, that was probably easy compared to the guy that did Pulp Fiction. Like: Wow, I got to change everybody’s perception about who I am. I don’t get a lot of offers, but it’s okay.

They don’t really make comedies anymore. Not like they used to. I don’t want to be [cast in the role of] the judge. Plus, I’m at this weird place. People are like, “How old is he?”

I’m older than Morgan Freeman was in Shawshank. I’m older than Danny Glover was in Lethal Weapon. You know what I mean? So it’s like: “Is he the guy, or is he like Michael Douglas in Ant-Man?” Like: You go get him, Antie.

Hey, I’ll do it. I’ll shine Michael B. Jordan’s guns. “All right. They’re ready. They’re ready.” I don’t give a fuck. If that’s where I am now, you got to make these adjustments. I’m just trying to stay in the league, man. So I don’t get 25 shots anymore. Now I’m just boxing out. I’m playing good defense. Come in off the bench.

Oh, I totally identify. I mean, I like to say there’s a part of me that’s been every character in the movie. So I’m her, I’m the agent, I’m my character. I’m Anna Kendrick, even. I’m everybody in there. And yeah, Misty’s going through what I just said. It is hard when people actually think they know who you are to give you another chance, to think you’re worthy of another chance. And she doesn’t make it easy for herself. You know what I mean?

I mean, not to that extent. But here’s the thing about self-destructive behavior. Can you be nice while you’re doing it? Some addicts are better than others. I’ve never been that guy. I’ve never been poison on a set. I would even say, and I say this about most actors, 40, 50 percent of your work’s going to be from friends, from people just going, “Hey, you know who’s really cool to hang out with? Chris.” You know what I mean?

I’ve been in that audition. And then Kadeem Hardison walked in the room. You’re like, Kadeem! When I write a Hollywood thing—and I’m not trying to diss anybody—I’ve actually worked jobs. Most of my friends that work in show business have never worked a fucking real job. And if they worked a real job, they were working their way through college, knowing good and well they weren’t going to be there [forever]. So they never really thought the job was going to be their life. So when I write Hollywood, I’m still writing the guy that worked at Red Lobster. I’m writing the guy that loaded trucks at the Daily News. These are jobs that I had. It’s not a Hollywood thing. It’s an everywhere thing.

Why’d I cast myself? I don’t know. I guess I could have given it to somebody. I did think about it. It’s just like, “Eh, it’s not that time yet.”

You know what? It was like a quick on-set thing, basically, so I’m not the same guy in Top Five. A lot of directors, a lot of Black directors, have this hat uniform. They have a hat, and the hat’s got the name on it. So it’s Spike. It was the Hughes brothers. It was Matty Rich. There’s this uniform in being a Black director sometimes. It’s my homage to Robert Townsend and Reggie Hudlin and Malcolm Lee, and all these guys.

I mean, a little. I had a brother who struggled with alcohol, yes. It’s a lot of other people I’ve met. We just have so much mental illness now. And there’s something about—it’s weird. When you’re the sibling of somebody like that, or even my brother, your friends, everybody around you, only sees the drunk person, only sees the manic schizophrenic person, but you always see the person you grew up with. You still remember this brother that was like your best friend, and you don’t give that up. No matter what behavior you see, you’re just holding on [to] all the hope in the world that you can get that brother back. And that’s what Misty goes through. A lot of people are like, “Well, just leave him.” It’s like, “Nah, man. You didn’t know him like I knew him.”

I know some dead people. I know a lot of dead people. How old are you?

I’ll give you about 12 years, 15 years. You start losing the people that just don’t eat right. Just as simple as that. It’s not even the addicts who start going. And it’s not even that they OD; it’s just at some point your body can’t fight this fight anymore. So [in your] 50s, you start losing people. You start losing people to natural causes sometimes. It’s crazy.

There’s a weird statistic I read a long time ago. Of the 45 presidents, like 35 of them lost a father or a parent early in life. It makes you grow up. It’ll make you or break you. So yeah, it sobered me up somewhat. My father died in ’88; ’90, I’m on SNL. You know what I mean? So it’s like, Get serious, figure it out. It’s time to figure it out.

I was successful, I guess. But you got to also remember, at that time, all of us were in the shadow of Eddie Murphy. That’s what success was.

How do I explain it? I bought a house a year and a half, maybe two years before, bought a carriage house in Brooklyn, and I couldn’t afford it. And so I just had to get onstage a lot, and I had to work every gig. You ever read the Gladwell book? The Beatles basically just did more shows than everybody. So it was the Beatles, the Kinks, all these other bands. And the Beatles had the worst boss. The Beatles just did way more shows than everybody. We try to make it into this mythical thing. It’s kind of the same thing, man. I bought a house, and I had to fucking get onstage. Two things happened. I had to get onstage to pay for this house, but I also, privately anyway, I had quit show business in a sense.

I had given up because I’d done CB4, I’d done New Jack City, I’d been on SNL, and I was like, “Okay, I’m going to just be a comedian.” Not that there was any shame to it, but my goal was to be George Wallace. George Wallace is a great comedian, and I love George Wallace because all he did was stand-up and he had a real schedule in his life. Most comedians have no schedule, right? George Wallace works from here to here. He goes on vacation these months of the year. I kind of, in the back of my mind, always wanted a family, always wanted kids. So that was my goal. I do this special, and it’s hard to even explain. The world went crazy.

Here’s a funny story. I got Bring the Pain. I have a VHS of Bring the Pain. I left my agent, and I left my manager, but I have Bring the Pain. Now nobody knows what it is. It’s very similar to Dre and Snoop walking around with The Chronic, trying to get a deal. And by the way, it’s around the same time. So I go to this agent. I’m not going to say his name, whatever. He’s made up with me since. I still got a little ego, and I’m like, “Hey, I’d like you to be my agent.” I give him the Bring the Pain tape. He watches it. He says, “It’s okay.” He goes, and I quote, “I got too many Black guys.” He said, “I got too many Black guys.” Whatever. Cut to two months later, Bring the Pain airs and it’s like this big thing. I’m on Oprah, I’m on 60 Minutes, and that agent calls me back, “Hey. I’ll handle you for 5 percent.”

I thought about it, but then I couldn’t do it. I couldn’t do it. I got too many Black guys. A guy actually said that to me.

Bigger & Blacker is bigger than Bring the Pain. It’s like, what if Bad sold more than Thriller? I got a nice body of work. I’m fine with Head of State, I’m fine with I Think I Love My Wife, [which are] the two films before Top Five, but I think I could have been more serious about directing. That’s the only thing I would say. I never let my ego mess up my stand-up. Every special, I put a ton of work into. Kill the Messenger, I remember Mike Nichols calling me and he said, “I like it, but you got onstage too much. It’s like: You worked it too much. And I can see at points you’re a little robotic. You don’t need to work it that hard.” But yeah, I was learning a lot of things on the fly. I didn’t know anything about money. Lorne Michaels said to me a long time ago, “Everybody loses their first money. But if you’re talented, you’ll make more.” I knew nothing about just the dynamics of fame and how it affected the people around you and all that stuff. It was a lot.

No, I’m not doing it for money. I mean, I’ll make money off of it, but the thing with Misty Green, what I realized when I did Top Five, it’s like: This is my lane as a filmmaker. I’d love to make Man on Fire or something. I would love to make fill-in-the-blank big-budget movie and have this big-budget Rush Hour–esque idea. Those guys are really good at that. It’s not really my thing. I make a tailored suit. My suits are made by hand, by one guy. And it’s okay. A little movie is what I should probably be doing, and it’s where my interest is. And some of those other movies I did was kind of me trying to get famous.

Robert De Niro’s like 84. He’s got a little baby. He’s my man. He’s got literally a two-year-old or something. I mean, I never plan too much ahead. I’m just trying to get as much work done as possible. Having kids that are grown, it seems like I got a little more time on my hands. So hopefully that results in more work. I’m probably going to direct more. I don’t know how much [more] stand-up I’m going to do.

I got like six, seven specials, man. That’s a lot. So I don’t know. I’m not announcing anything or anything, but if I do it, I want to do it right. In sports, especially in football, they always talk about separation. “Can he get separation?” You know what I mean? “Yeah, he’s fast, but is he fast enough? Can he get separation?” And that’s the way I feel, like, as far as stand-up. As long as I can get separation, I’ll do it. Yeah, I’m going to write. That’s basically what it boils down to. Wake up, write. That’s it. Just write, write, write, write, write. Get it all out. ✦

#6715. 3 Key Takeaways From Lagos Fashion Week

Africa’s biggest and buzziest fashion week drew to a close on Sunday night with an intimate dinner held by Nigerian heavyweight designer Lisa Folawiyo, who returned to the official Lagos Fashion Week schedule after a seven-year break. The five-day event saw approximately 16,000 people in attendance, up from 15,000 last season. Some 65 designers flocked to the Nigerian metropolis to showcase their collections to an audience of press, influencers, and other industry figures.

This season, it was local talent who dominated the week, with several Nigerian designers showcasing their collections on and off-schedule. As with all Lagos Fashion Week events, shows happen on-site at the Federal Palace Hotel, while off-site shows take place around the city. Mainstay designers like Emmy Kasbit, Ugo Monye, and Sisano showcased their collections through a mix of presentations and runway shows. Other buzzy designers such as Hertunba welcomed guests to their new stores (in addition to their runway shows), while LFJ held her Spring/Summer 2027 runway at her concept store Akoko.

Even those who now show up at fashion week internationally like Iamisigo, who showcased her collection in Copenhagen, and Orange Culture and Fruché, who both presented their collections in Berlin, are committed to returning and being a part of the Lagos Fashion Week calendar, too.

Now in its 16th edition, the platform is gaining more international attention than ever before. International buyers and media were in town from the Middle East as well as neighboring African countries including Senegal and Ghana, while buzzy US influencers and models Eni Popoola and Alton Mason also flew in for the shows.

(Left) Jermaine Bleu, and Boyedoe (right).

During the week, guests gathered at the US General Consulate to witness Omoyemi Akerele, founder of Lagos Fashion Week, receive an Excellence in Commercial and Creative Leadership Award from Consul General Brandon Hudspeth. Guests included Chioma Ude, founder of Africa International Film Festival, influencers Popoola and Akin Faminu, as well as designers like Ejiro Amos Tafiri. The award signifies Lagos Fashion Week’s ability to help springboard talent into the international market, particularly in the US.

“[Akerele] has built a platform that brings Nigerian fashion to the world,” said Consul General Hudspeth during Friday’s event. “American talent has found a home right here in Lagos. Last year, singer Ciara was right here making headlines on the Lagos runway during fashion week.” He also points to brands like US’s Tia Adeola and Studio 189, a label co-founded by actress Rosario Dawson, which have shown on the Lagos schedule.

Omoyemi Akerele, founder of Lagos Fashion Week receiving an award from Brandon Hudspeth, the Consul General.

Beyond the runway, Nigerian designers are going global, Hudspeth acknowledged. “Nigerian designers are reaching American customers, and that creates business for Americans and Nigerians,” he added, pointing to New York-based e-commerce platform Moda Operandi, which holds digital trunk shows for Lagos Fashion Week designers, and trade shows like Coterie, which has featured local talent. “This, of course, is cultural diplomacy, but it is also commercial diplomacy, and the consulate is working to build these relations and connections.”

African designers who have spent more than two decades in the industry returned to the schedule, including Christie Brown and Lisa Folawiyo, as well as Bridget Awosika from Nigeria. “I feel it’s important that we were within the official calendar. It makes sense,” said Folawiyo. “It’s something I really thought about and I felt this is the right time.” The brand, which turned 21 years old this year, brought Lagos Fashion Week to a close with a candle lit five-course meal, surrounded by an intimate crowd of celebrities, influencers, friends and industry leaders.

For Ghana’s Christie Brown, returning to Lagos Fashion Week after an eight-year hiatus was part of a larger expansion strategy as the brand builds its presence across the continent. “As much as we’re building a global brand, we also do believe that there are certain key markets on the continent that we absolutely need to have a presence in,” said founder and creative director Aisha Ayensu. Those hotspots include Kenya, Côte d’Ivoire, Nigeria, Ghana, and South Africa. “This is a re-entry into the market. We don’t want to come in guns blazing. We want to enter cautiously.” The brand now has a six-month residency at luxury retailer Temple Muse, giving local consumers an opportunity to shop Christie Brown pieces in Lagos.

Ugo Monye, the founder of his eponymous label, returned after a year-long break. The popular Nigerian designer explained that there’s an overwhelming pressure to create and prioritize design. Many simply enjoy the design process and do not pay attention to whether the backend business operations are in order. Unlike in the West, where designers are creating collections for four or more seasons, Monye and several African designers prefer to do one collection a year. He said his collections from two seasons ago are still in demand.

“Because I was having some backend issues, the workload was a lot and then to add fashion week on top of it, I just said, ‘You know what? Let me just take a break and catch my breath, then come back,’” he said, adding that he is the only person on his team overseeing the business. “Our industry is not fully structured yet, so you have to be a part of everything, even when you hire people.”

Despite the break, Monye is committed to showcasing in Lagos. “I’m not going anywhere. I’m here for a long time,” he said. “The brand [leaving] the fashion week calendar is out of the question.”

Showing during Lagos Fashion Week is increasingly important because of the rising media attention, said Abelia Anaba Franklyn, founder of couture house Weiz Dhurm Franklyn. “[Designers] want more coverage. It’s such an important moment in fashion, African fashion and Nigerian fashion,” she said. “Nigerians have the spending power. Once you have a distinct point of view that is not a regurgitation of another brand, people will acclimate toward you.” Now, the couturier is branching further into ready-to-wear where her pieces start from $600.

Elsewhere, others used fashion week as an opportunity to announce major business news. On Saturday, Post-Imperial shared that it was shutting down after 10 years. “I’ve said everything I needed to say with Post-Imperial,” said founder Niyi Okuboyejo backstage at his final show, which was a collaboration with Nigerian sustainable fashion brand This Is Us. Over the past decade, the brand built a strong wholesale model and was in over 200 retail stores, from Bergdorf Goodman in the US to Alára in Nigeria.

“Today’s a great day for me,” he added. “I also tried to expand the idea of what fashion is, and fashion shows aren’t necessarily just runway.” With this final collection, held in the courtyard, Okuboyejo gathered friends of the brands to walk the makeshift runway, including stylist Ugo Mozie, industrial designer Nifemi Marcus-Bello, and Dada Gallery’s Oyinkan Dada.

There’s often a misconception that Lagos Fashion Week is just for Nigerian designers. While they make up the majority, there are a handful of designers from across the continent who traveled to cash in on the buzz. This season saw some new and old international designers join the schedule, including Ghana’s Christie Brown and IGC Fashion from Uganda.

Unable to secure sponsorships in time, IGC Fashion self-funded its trip to Lagos Fashion Week, hoping to connect with media, a new audience and a larger fashion market. “We’re lacking media and big investors in the country. It’s a big opportunity for designers in Uganda to be at a stage like Lagos Fashion Week,” said brand founder Katende Godfrey.

Over in North Africa, Moroccan designer Scheherazade Essrhir shares a similar sentiment. After participating in Lagos Fashion Week’s Green Access, an incubator for young designers, Essrhir took some time away to perfect her craft. “Through Green Access, I learnt that being a designer is more than creating and designing. It’s a lot of work,” she said. “[At Lagos Fashion Week], they support us even when the show is over.” In Lagos, Essrhir feels she has support and community as the fashion week team schedules regular check-in calls and feedback.

From a business lens, South African designer Mzukisi Mbane, founder of Imprint ZA, believes Lagos is the place to be. “In South Africa, we have fashion shows. We have the glitz and the glamour. But for me, the bottom line is always important,” he said. “I want to be visible to people that can help the brand grow and be seen… even if [buyers] are not purchasing pieces, I’m still on their radar.” Mbane was named a recipient of this year’s Africa Fashion Up Award, an initiative dedicated to nurturing emerging regional designers, and will see him receive mentorship from Balenciaga, since the Kering-owned brand has on-going partnership with the platform.

British Nigerian designer Reni Abina chose to bring her collection to Lagos again this season. “As we expand internationally, it’s important to me that we remain connected to the city and the community that first embraced us,” Abina said. “We’ve always wanted to build a truly global fashion brand, but I don’t believe that global recognition should come at the expense of our roots.”

There were a handful of buyers in attendance this season, many of whom noticed a shift in the overall collections on display. “I’ve been coming [to Lagos Fashion Week] for a few years, and this is probably the most cohesive year that I’ve ever experienced,” says Arinola Fagbemi, a buyer at Lagos-based concept store Alara, adding that they are now building collections around who their client is and what they might want to buy from them.

Wearability is a key concern. This season, Alara partnered up with Lagos Fashion Week to host a showroom for designers after their runway shows. It’s a move that’s really helped buyers, including the Alara team, see the clothes in-person and gauge things like finishing, texture, and weight. Standout shows for her include Orange Culture, Dukun, and Orire. “We’re looking for the finishing. Clients are very discerning, especially the Alara client. They want things that are well made. They don’t care that it’s from Nigeria or from Africa. They expect the same level of detail,” she says.

African retailers are setting aside a separate budget for Lagos. “We’ve understood now that it works differently,” says Fagbemi, adding they do not follow the international buying calendar and place orders for every season. “The fortunate thing is that the turnaround time for a lot of African brands is very quick. So what we’re seeing on the runway now, many of them will have it ready for the holidays, because of Detty December [a festive period full of parties and live music events] and that peak period.” Alara buyers also attend Milan, London and Paris fashion weeks.

Viva Accra operates on a different model. “We have an allocation for African designers within our overall buying budget, rather than a completely separate budget for Lagos. It’s about finding the right brands and making considered buying decisions,” says Sacha Okoh, creative director and buyer at Viva Accra, a concept store in Ghana.

Lagos Fashion Week is an important discovery platform. “We have a genuine interest in growing our African designer offering,” continues Okoh, noting that the store currently carries a number of Nigerian and Ghanaian brands, but she is “always looking for designers whose work I feel can sit comfortably alongside our international labels.”

She adds: “A collection can be beautiful on the runway, but for me, it’s also about how those pieces translate into real wardrobes. I look for that balance between creativity, quality, wearability and commercial appeal.” Standout collections include Christie Brown, Jermaine Bleu and Boyedoe. Okoh regularly attends fashion weeks and trade shows in Milan, Paris, and London.

As Sunny Dolat, a researcher, consultant and Lagos Fashion Week SS27’s creative director, observes: “This year, the platform attracted an even larger international audience than last, with many visitors traveling to Nigeria specifically for fashion week,” he says. “This strongly indicates a platform that is not only well regarded and respected, but has firmly established itself as an important destination for discovering some of the most compelling design talent from across the African continent.”

#6714. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6712. Who Is Elizabeth Holmes’s Partner, Billy Evans?

This story contains spoilers for You Can See Everything.

When Nathan Fielder asked Elizabeth Holmes to document the days leading up to her serving her prison sentence for his new A24 documentary, You Can See Everything, the proposition meant that he would also be spending a large portion of the shoot with Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans.

The documentary spends time delving into Holmes’s public legal scandal with Theranos—the now-defunct biotech company that saw her committing investment fraud—but it also sheds light on Holmes and Evans’s relationship and how they have managed to thrive despite her sentencing.

As the documentary, co-directed by Lance Oppenheim, progresses, Fielder’s focus shifts from Holmes to Evans. “Weren’t you worried she was scamming you?” Fielder asked him at one point, to which Evans responded, “100 percent, but what does she have to gain from me?” When presented with the knowledge of his family’s wealth, Evans defended Holmes and said, “I think there’s a lot of different levels of wealth.” Things only snowball from there.

Evans’s grandparents, William and Anne Evans, own the Evans Hotel Group. Founded in 1953, Evans Hotels consists of three luxury properties, which include The Lodge Terry Pines, the Bahia Resort Hotel, and the Catamaran Resort Hotel and Spa. All three of the properties are located in California.

Evans’s LinkedIn profile revealed that he attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology between 2011 and 2015. He earned his bachelor’s degree in economics.

Evans’s LinkedIn also revealed that he’s the CEO of Haemanthus, his self-founded AI-driven medical testing startup; he’s held the role since 2022. The company aims to achieve a mission similar to that of Holmes’s Theranos, which sought to provide blood diagnostics through one drop of blood with the Edison machine. Instead of using one drop of blood for diagnostics, Haemanthus is working to create a device that tests blood in addition to urine and saliva for the presence of diseases.

“This is not Theranos 2.0. Theranos attempted to miniaturize existing tests. Our approach is fundamentally different. We use light to read the complete molecular story in biological fluids, seeing patterns current tests can’t detect. Not an improvement. A different paradigm,” the company shared in a statement to Fortune in 2025, following reports of Holmes advising on the project. “Setting the record straight. Elizabeth Holmes has zero involvement in Haemanthus. We’ve learned from her company’s mistakes, but she has no role, now or future.”

In a 2023 joint interview with The New York Times, Evans revealed that he and Holmes fell for each other fast. “To say we immediately fell in love isn’t an overstatement,” he said.

Holmes, however, noted that Evans had some reservations about entering a relationship with her. “It had been two years of all this stuff written about me, and I think you get to know someone in a totally different way when you walk in with that skepticism versus if you meet when everything is sunshine and roses,” she said. “That allowed us to get to know each other in a really deep way.” The couple got engaged in August 2018.

Holmes gave birth to their son, William Holmes Evans, in 2021. By 2023, a court document revealed that Holmes gave birth to her and Evans’s second child, a daughter named Invicta.

Evans attended several of Holmes’s court dates, appearing by her side on the way to and from her hearings. In January 2022, she was found guilty of three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud. She’s currently serving her sentence—which was reduced to nine years from 11 years—at Federal Prison Camp Bryan in Texas. She will be transferred to a halfway house in August 2027.

While Holmes was sentenced, Evans asked the court in November 2022 to shorten her sentence so she could enjoy more special moments with their son. “My heart is broken with the thought of spending any days away from Liz, for a future in which my son grows up with a relationship with his mother on the other side of glass armed by guards,” he said. Evans still visits Holmes regularly, with him telling People in February 2025 that it has been “hell and torture” at the prison facility. The tech CEO added that it “shatters” Holmes when she says goodbye to him and her family.

You Can See Everything makes some shocking revelations about Evans, like that he posts from Holmes’s X account while she’s in prison (for a while, it was without her knowledge), and that he arranged to be paid for his and Holmes’s appearance in the documentary, which he ultimately rescinded. (It’s unclear whether Holmes knew about the deal.)

During a screening of the film in L.A. this month, Fielder said of the couple, “Neither of them have seen the film. Elizabeth is still incarcerated; Billy hasn’t seen it.” He added, according to The Hollywood Reporter, that Evans “started trying to exert a level of control over the process that made it very hard to engage with him, and it was uncomfortable for us and also A24 and everyone. And I think we sort of had to stop—I think communication broke down basically, and we’ve been in that like state for a little bit. So it’s been challenging in that way.”

Evans confirmed that he hasn’t seen the film during an interview with the All In podcast, which was released on October 15. “I haven’t seen it. I might think this is the dumbest thing I have ever done,” Evans said, per Variety. He has seen the trailer and said that Holmes “looks insane” in it. Evans added, “Am I nervous? I have been through so many intense, surreal experiences that it takes a bit to raise my blood pressure. With this, there’s certainly concern, but it’s ultimately our decision.”

On November 3, Evans revealed the “one misconception” about his relationship with Holmes following the release of the movie: “That I somehow control Liz. Anyone who actually knows her would find that idea hilarious,” he responded to an X user.

Evans added, “She’s fiercely independent, strong willed, and my best friend. We are partners in every sense. We challenge each other, disagree, and face the world together. Her closest friends are also some of my closest friends. If I ever mistreated her, they’d have my head.”

In a separate tweet, Evans revealed that he misses “everything about [Holmes].” He wrote, “I miss her presence. Her touch. The way she runs her fingers through my hair. Her patience. She makes me a better person. And without her, I feel an emptiness that’s hard to describe. People often say they need someone when what they really mean is that they want them. I’ve thought a lot about that distinction. I need Liz. She should qualify as a medically necessary prescription.”

On All In, Evans elaborated on why he wanted to make the film ahead of Holmes’s 11-year sentence. “She’s been prevented from speaking publicly in any way, shape, or form, and this would come out after that period in which she is now allowed to talk,” he said. “There’s been a lot of media produced on her. There’s been a lot of people who have told her story. That narrative is pretty ossified. The whole idea was: Here she is, see her and make up your own mind. It’s not to re-litigate the case. Practically, at this time she was not allowed to talk about the case, so she was gonna follow the rules and not talk about the case.”

He explained that his own loved ones have thought he was “crazy” for knowing—and now being in a relationship with—Holmes. “And they would meet her and spend time with her and see her in a totally natural environment, like going on a hike or helping a friend. Every opinion of her would radically shift,” Evans said. “That was the intention of the film. To help scale that up and allow other people to sit with her and make up their own minds.”

#6710. Zoë Kravitz Goes “Coco Suede” for Fall

A hair transformation doesn’t have to be dramatic to make a big splash. Just take actor Zoë Kravitz, whose subtle color tweak this month is bound for fall mood boards everywhere.

Called “coco suede” by Rita Hazan, the celebrity colorist and salon owner behind the change, Kravtiz’s warm new shade is a departure for the star, who has gone for cool-toned deep shades and icy platinum in the past.

“Coco suede is warm but neutral, not red or brassy,” Hazan says. “It gives her skin tone a sun-like glow.”

Kravitz debuted the shade on the set of Die Alive, a forthcoming dark romantic comedy written and directed by Megan Park (My Old Ass, Sterling Point). “I did it a few weeks ago for the movie role she is doing now,” Hazan confirms.

We’ll be keeping an eye out for further details on the project—but until then, Kravitz’s new color is setting a cozy tone for the cooler months.

#6707. Owen Wilson Breaks Down the World’s Best Golf Courses

The PGA Tour may be wrapping up in just a few short weeks, but this week marks the official beginning of Stick Season. No, not the Noah Kahan song, but Owen Wilson’s charming Apple TV+ comedy, whose second season premieres this Wednesday, November 4th. The show follows Wilson’s Pryce “Stick” Cahill, a former pro golfer who crashed out in a Kenny Powers-esque blaze of almost-glory a couple decades ago. Season one tracked his reentry into the game as the mentor of a talented but troubled young golfer played by Peter Dager. But in Season two, Stick has his eyes on a new prize: becoming the oldest player to ever win the U.S. Open.

Wilson himself might not be winning majors any time soon, but his experience filming the show has turned him into a real golf nut. He hadn’t played much beforehand, he told me, so the last couple of years have been a real crash course in one of the most difficult sports in the world. Still, it hasn’t taken much for him to compile a list of his favorite courses—and a bucket list of ones he’s dying to play a round or two on. Ahead of the show’s return, the 57-year-old actor hit the links with GQ.

“I have gotten an invite from a member to play, so I think that will happen at some point. What's always funny about that is that they close right after The Masters, so they're closed all summer. I’ve got to find a time that works for them where I could go play. That would be incredible.”

“My brother says St. Andrews and some of the other courses in Scotland are incredible. Out there the links style is pretty different from the courses in Dallas. And the people in Scotland, Luke says, are so knowledgeable about the game and friendly. I have not played link style and sometimes I wonder, Well, maybe my game would suit that because sometimes I'm not getting a lot of lift on the ball. And I am very comfortable with a putter. So yeah, maybe that's where I'll really prove that I'm good at the game.”

“Playing in Makena on Maui, that's a beautiful course that I love playing where you're getting to see the ocean and the beautiful Hawaiian features.”

“I played this one in Sydney that's kind of their [version of] Pebble Beach. It’s on the ocean, and there are some dramatic holes where you see waves breaking. I played lousy that day, but I'd like another crack at it.”

“I remember asking Collin Morikawa what his favorite course was and he said Riviera. Getting to play Riviera, I kind of feel like I've gotten to know more about the game. But now that I'm getting better, I can appreciate how incredible that course is. That first hole, where you're kind of teeing off from way up above. Just the other day, on number 10, I had a par four where I drove the green and just barely made it to the front of the green. But I was immediately on the phone calling to let my brothers and friends know that I had an eagle putt, which I missed. But that kind of kicked off a good little stretch where I birdied three out of four holes. That was a rare kind of day. More often, I'm kind of experiencing how challenging golf is.”

“I’ve stayed [at the Manor] and the course where they’re going to hold the Ryder Cup next year looked beautiful.”

“When I was training for the show, I learned how to play at Maui Country Club, a little nine-hole course kind of near where I am on the North Shore. [Maui] and Mākena, those were the two places that I really played a lot.”

“I played my best round at King Kamehameha with [former NBA coach] Don Nelson. I'd only been playing for a year-and-a-half where I was able to shoot in the low 80s, and everything just was very simple that day. Like, you hit your drive on the fairway, and then on the fairway you just hit it on the green, and then you two-putt and move on. I was with Nellie when he got his last hole in one. At that point I think he was maybe 83, and he was able to shoot his age and get a hole in one. I have not gotten a hole in one yet, but it's very exciting to witness one.”

#6705. Colin Jost Takes Gift-Giving Seriously

The Weekend Update co-host and Kay campaign star shares his approach to holiday shopping.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Finding the perfect holiday gift isn’t easy. Between the pressure to get it right, the endless wish lists, and the people who insist they don’t want anything, shopping for loved ones can feel like an impossible mission. Even Colin Jost, who has spent years navigating the pressures of live television, admits that the process is incredibly stressful.

This festive season, the Weekend Update co-host is putting his comedic talents to work with Kay by starring in the jeweler’s latest holiday campaign, “Love All In.” The cheeky ad follows Jost on an increasingly ridiculous quest to find the perfect present, poking fun at the lengths we’ll go to for the people closest to us. It’s a fitting partnership for someone who knows a thing or two about making people laugh but also takes gifting pretty seriously.

“I think I’m a good gift giver,” Jost tells ELLE. “Giving gifts is stressful because I do want it to be a meaningful gift. I hate the idea of just buying something because you have to give someone something.”

For Jost, the secret to getting it right has less to do with how much you spend and more to do with how much thought goes into it. “At every kind of price point for any gift, there [are] thoughtful and unthoughtful versions,” he says. “Something can be really expensive but not thoughtful.”

It’s a sentiment that aligns with Kay’s latest campaign, which encourages shoppers to go “all in” when expressing their love. And while Jost might not be the first person you’d think to turn to for jewelry advice, he’s developed an appreciation for it over the years, thanks to his very chic wife, Scarlett Johansson.

“Until five years ago, I didn’t own a watch,” he admits. That changed when the actress gifted him his first one, introducing him to an entirely new world of accessories. As for whether she’s influenced his personal style? “In that it’s exclusively managed by her, yes, I would say she’s influenced it.”

Despite his Staten Island roots, Jost’s jewelry preferences are surprisingly understated. “I don’t really wear a ton of jewelry, but I also am from Staten Island, so I do have to have certain pieces, or else they won’t let me back over the Verrazano Bridge,” he jokes.

While browsing Kay’s assortment, he found himself drawn to simple gold pieces, including a ring, bracelet, and necklace. “They were really nice, but also they weren’t gaudy or anything,” he says. His preference for gold also comes with some rather unconventional reasoning: “If we get into a post-apocalyptic situation, it feels like it’s better to melt down for trading.”

When it comes to shopping for the people closest to him, Jost admits that both Johansson and his Weekend Update collaborator Michael Che are difficult to buy things for, though he found a creative solution for the latter. “I got Che a really large and heavy, realistic statue of a velociraptor,” he recalls. “It was so heavy that he literally can’t get rid of it.” The real expense wasn’t the dinosaur itself. “The main cost was shipping,” he says. “It was a huge eyesore, and it’s prohibitively expensive for him to have removed from his property.”

The hardest person to gift on Jost’s list? His father, who insists he doesn’t need anything. “I think he actually means it, but it’s so unhelpful,” Jost says. After years of nostalgic gifts inspired by his dad’s past, he’s running out of ideas. “I’ve got to figure out something that breaks through his defenses.”

In terms of gifting etiquette, Jost has a few rules of his own. For starters, he’s big on surprises. While he understands the appeal of a wish list for children, he thinks adults should leave a little room for the unexpected. “For adults, it’s got to be ‘surprise me,’” he says. “The surprise is half the fun, three-quarters of the fun.” Regifting, on the other hand, comes with a few conditions. He’s open to the idea, but only if the gift is a perfect fit for someone and there’s full disclosure.

But perhaps the most surprising revelation comes when I ask what’s on his own holiday wish list. After spending much of our conversation discussing what to buy everyone else, Jost seems relieved to finally be on the receiving end. “Oh, thank you! Finally, someone asked me. What do I want?”

His answer? Nothing material. “At this point in life, I mostly want experiences,” he says. Whether it’s a trip or simply someone taking the initiative to organize an outing, he’s more interested in making memories than collecting more things. “Even if it’s just the plan of, ‘Let’s go do this at this time,’ I think that’s a great gift.” Or, when in doubt, a velociraptor.

#6700. 16 Best Automatic Watches for Men 2026, According to GQ Watch Nerds

A budding “watch guy” most likely starts off their collection with an assortment of quartz tickers (and let’s be clear, there’s nothing wrong with that). But as your interest in watches grows, it’s only natural for you to want something on your wrist you can brag about, which inevitably pushes you towards automatic watches.

Inside the case of an automatic watch is a weighted rotor that spins as you move your arm, a few little flicks of your wrist throughout the day keeps the internal mechanisms running long enough to keep that minute hand tick-tick-ticking across the dial.

But automatic watches also have a reputation for being finicky or costly. And while that can be true, the beauty of watches is the wide price scale in which the industry operates. From stunners for less than $250 to ones you’d have to mortgage your house (and maybe your parents’ house) to buy, here are the top automatic watches on the market today for any budget.

While not impossible to find a great watch at the $250-mark, you are going to be limited. Given the many internal pieces and complicated mechanisms needed to build an automatic watch, many brands have to charge a bit more for a quality automatic. Even so, brands like Orient and Seiko lead the way on well-made (and well-designed) options.

Orient’s range of inexpensive watches punch well above their weight-class and the Symphony III is no different. With its classic, clean design and movement that promises 40 hours of power reserve, this is a watch that’s made to be a daily driver without breaking the bank.

Timex’s Waterbury is a staple in their line-up and the extremely stylish Metrograph has an Art Deco-style case and dial that’s pared-down enough to keep things simple, but without looking boring.

The Seiko 5 is something of a cult favorite for the Japanese brand – and for good reason. It’s a perfect daily driver and a budget-friendly alternative to the Rolex Datejust. Best of all, it clocks in at just 37mm, which is the perfect case size for nearly any wrist.

As ever, Timex provides maximum bang for minimum buck with this classic "Pepsi" bezel diver.

At $500, the doorway starts to open up a bit more – but only a creak. The usual suspects like Timex and Casio, are populating this price point, Bulova and Sternglas are great alternatives who will give you a little more street cred among collectors.

Undoubtedly one of the best looking watches in the sub-$500 category, the Timex Marlin in this particular shade of green strikes the perfect balance between classic and modern.

Heavily influenced by motorsports, the Edifice is a bit of a departure from the digital, retro-charm of many mainstays for Casio. The integrated bracelet keeps it sporty, while the patterned dial makes it a little more interesting than other options on the market.

At 45mm, 200-meter of water resistance, and 42-hours of power reserve, the Bulova Marine Star ticks all the boxes for a great dive watch at a reasonable price – the two-toned bezel is just a nice bonus.

This fan favorite hits the bullseye of the style-quality-price nexus, and looks especially fetching with a bright yellow dial.

A thousand bucks is a perfectly reasonable budget to have when you want to upgrade your watch game without completely breaking the bank. Here, I’d recommend looking at smaller, or more indie brands to find some interesting designs not seen by more household names.

You’d be forgiven for not knowing their name, but Kuoe is starting to gain traction in the U.S.. The Japanese-based watchmaker produces high-quality, well-designed pieces that harken to a more classic watch style. The OLD SMITH is based on the military field watch, but with a slightly more refined design language.

A reborn grail from the Studio 54 era, with a vintage-correct 35mm case.

UNIMATIC uses the basic field watch as the springboard for their Modello Due, which strips it back to its barebones to make something a bit bolder, a bit more modern, and eye-catching.

Paulin is a Glasgow-based microbrand that’s known for colorful, unique, and whimsical watches, often playing with color to make their designs all the more interesting.

Needless to say, if money isn’t an issue, the sky’s the limit. Not all watches are created equal and buying just for the name recognition alone doesn’t always make for the best watch for the money. Instead, look for a price point that’s commensurate with the movement, design, and materials used, and you’ll never regret the decision to spend the big bucks.

Taken from a 1924 archival design, the Brunswick’s cushion case, clean lines, and mother-of-pearl dial may all feel a bit “precious”, shall we say; but this is a workhorse watch that’s destined to be a daily driver for anyone who is looking for a little eye-candy on the wrist.

The IWC Ingenieur is a masterfully made ceramic watch (and matching ceramic bracelet) that will no doubt get you a few compliments every time you wear it to the office.

Not many watches can be mistaken for a Bell & Ross watch with its larger proportions and signature square case shape. The BR-05, the brand’s most popular model, is a sportier, slightly bolder answer to Cartier’s Santos.

It’s hard to narrow down one Grand Seiko to choose, but the White Birch is subtle and versatile enough to dress up or use as your daily driver. Most impressive about this particular model is the Caliber 9SA5 movement, which promises a whopping 80-hours of power when fully wound – nearly twice that of many others on the market.

Mechanical watch movements fall into two basic categories: hand-wound and automatic. Before the invention of automatic wristwatches in the 1920s (and long before the invention of battery-powered quartz movements in the 1960s) all watches were hand-wound. That meant you needed to manually wind up your watch every day to keep it running. An automatic watch (also called a self-winding watch) doesn’t require this because it winds automatically with the movement of your body as you wear it.

Most automatic watches wind themselves via a weighted rotor, which you’ll be able to see if your watch has a see-through case back (it’s the half moon-shaped piece right on top). When you wear the watch and move around, the rotor winds a spring, which turns the hands, date wheel and everything else that moves on a watch.

To keep your watch from stopping when you’re sitting still (or when you take it off at night) automatic movements also store excess energy and slowly release it over hours or days while the rotor is stationary. This is called a “power reserve,” and it typically ranges from 40 to 80 hours, with some going as high as a week or more. They’re useful if you don’t wear a watch every day, and don’t want to have to reset the date and time every time you put it on—particularly with annual or perpetual calendar models that can be complicated to set.

It’s not a downside, per se, but they do require some upkeep. Unlike a quartz watch that requires nothing more than a new battery every few years, a mechanical watch is a finely-tuned machine consisting of many tiny, precisely calibrated parts. Watchmakers have made huge advances in shock-and waterproofing over the years, but there’s still only so much abuse a mechanical movement can take. And that’s the thing: repairs to automatic watches can be expensive.

If you stick to the manufacturer’s recommended service schedule (it’ll need an overhaul and lube every 4 to 10 years, depending on the brand and model) and don’t make a habit of wearing it in the sauna, you’ll probably be fine. Whether it’s a $200 Amazon special or a $200,000 grand complication, automatic watches are designed to be worn, so the best way to take care of your watch is to wear it as much as possible.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6699. At the NYPL’s Library Lions Gala, a Night Celebrating Libraries and Democracy

There’s just one night of the year when the majestic steps outside the New York Public Library on Fifth Avenue are covered in candles as opposed to tourists; when the metal detectors in Astor Hall are momentarily replaced by cocktail high-tops; when the long oak study tables in the historic Rose Main Reading Room are transformed into tablescapes laden with crimson roses and peonies. It is, of course, the Library Lions gala.

On Monday, guests made their way to the beloved institution for the annual black-tie affair that raises funds to sustain the library’s mission to support its 92 locations and inspire lifelong learning, while honoring notable literary figures in the arts, culture, and letters. This year’s line-up recognized the contributions of Joy Harjo, Stephen King, George Packer, Aaron Sorkin, Martha Stewart, and Jesmyn Ward.

Held on the eve of Election Day, the evening also carried an emphatic plea: support the library, perform your civic duty, and in doing so, champion democracy. “As we gather in this turbulent moment, on the precipice of what we’re told is no less than a dawn of a new technological age, your presence here tonight and your support for the New York Public Library is a strong statement and commitment to timeless, humanistic values,” said Abby Milstein, chair of the Board of Trustees of the New York Public Library, in her opening speech. “The library embraces the potential of the new age while it stands strong as a [haven for] free expression,  knowledge, and learning…and access and opportunity for all of it.”

Anthony Marx, president of the New York Public Library, echoed her sentiment. “We are and will remain the source of trustworthy information. All too rare these days, trustworthy information as a public good is the foundation of an informed democracy, which will be relevant tomorrow and the foundation for everyone’s economic opportunity,” he said. “Millions depend on us.”

The program continued with a video featuring all six newly minted Lions, where Sorkin said it best: “I think libraries are one of the fundamental institutions, not just of a literate society but of a democracy. And the less we invest in them, the more we try to use political power to control what’s in them, the weaker our democracy becomes.”

To drive home the message, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer took to the stage to deliver one final statement, which was met with thunderous applause. “Libraries provide a place open to all where anyone can learn facts through knowledge or just be excited and entertained by a great book, as I was on so many visits to the library when I was young,” he said. “But sadly, across America, fact and logic are under threat. So many in our country want to whitewash our history, censor our teachers, and force libraries to ban books. Let me tell you this: Banning books ain’t going to fly in New York or in America.”

Make no mistake: The evening was still a joyful celebration of the awe one experiences from reading and the community one finds in a library. Packer described it as “a charge.” “When you go into a library, you’re surrounded by strangers, and everyone’s focused on whatever they’re doing, but because we’re human, we look up at each other,” he said. “It’s that exchange of looks across the table.”

There was certainly some kind of charge in the air when King met his wife at the Fogler Library in Maine. “I asked her, ‘Do you ever read science fiction?’ And she said, ‘Yes, I do,’ and things progressed from there,” he recalled. “I’m not saying the library is anybody’s version of Tinder, but it’s a nice place to be.”

Indeed, the library—and the Reading Room, especially—is worth its weight in gold. Ward remembers walking into the Reading Room for the first time and finding herself “speechless.” “I think I felt that feeling of safety, but also wonder at the collection of knowledge and stories,” she added.

The gala also paid tribute to the late Dolly Parton, renowned not only as a remarkable performer, but as one of the nation’s greatest advocates for furthering access to reading. To date, Parton’s Imagination Library has gifted over 300 million books across the nation. By the end of the evening, a string quartet played renditions of her hits while attendees were ushered out of the Reading Room and into the after-party in Astor Hall, hosted by the Young Lions.

It was hard not to be captivated by how much the library had transformed throughout the evening and in between spaces, and by the presence of so many people and their stories—all contained in its hallowed halls. That turned out to be one of the biggest takeaways of the night: “You trust the library, right?” said Harjo. “There’s a lot of power there in a place that gathers together…the stories and the history and culture of peoples. We need to figure out a story together that includes everyone that also tells the truth.”

Alexandra Brunjes, Megan Zuckerman, Tobili Hatcher, Miranda Josephson
