These are the best-of-the-best bites for Minhaj, which is coincidentally the name of his new movie—Best of the Best, streaming now on Netflix—that he cowrote and produced with Prashanth Venkataramanujam and stars in as a professor and former dancer. The film pays homage to real-life Bollywood competitions, following collegiate dancers Maya and Anjali (played by Maitreyi Ramakrishnan and Priyanka Kedia, respectively), whose characters were inspired by “deeply passionate college kids in the biggest world that a lot of people have never heard of.”

Paleoproteomic analysis of fossils from northern China reveals that Denisovans had a distinctive physical appearance.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The enigmatic and now-extinct Denisovans of China shared traits with Neanderthals, modern humans and Homo erectus, according to a new study that looked at ancient proteins and fossils. But the Denisovans also had several unique skull traits and genetic variants that made them a distinctive ancient human group, according to the researchers ‪—‬ and these traits have now revealed a new face for a Denisovan man.

In the study, published Oct. 21 in the journal Nature, researchers analyzed Denisovan skulls from the archaeological site of Xujiayao in northern China. The Denisovans were a group of ancient humans who lived in Asia and disappeared around 30,000 years ago. This human relative was first identified in 2010 from the DNA of a finger bone discovered in a cave in Siberia.

The Xujiayao bones and teeth were excavated in the late 1970s, long before scientists knew about the existence of Denisovans, and were initially thought to be either Neanderthals or archaic Homo sapiens due to the shape of the fossils and their age: 138,000 to 199,000 years old.

But recent advances in paleoproteomics ‪—‬ the study of bone and tooth proteins that persist longer than DNA ‪—‬ have helped researchers identify Denisovan individuals due to specific genetic variants that differentiate them from other ancient human groups.

In the new study, researchers used paleoproteomic analysis on 20 remains from Xujaiyao and determined that all of them were from Denisovans. This determination then allowed the researchers to study the skull bones closely and figure out what Denisovans might have looked like.

The Xujiayao skulls had some features similar to H. erectus, the researchers wrote, including a low and wide braincase and thick cranial bones. But they also had anatomical features more similar to those of Neanderthals and modern humans, particularly in their bicuspids (the teeth between the canines and molars). The researchers also identified some unique Denisovan cranial traits. The back of the skull, for example, was more vertical and less rounded than in Neanderthals or modern humans.

Armed with a better understanding of Denisovan skull shape from the Xujiayao fossils, the researchers compared them with East Asian Denisovan remains that some experts have assigned to other species, such as Homo juluensis and Homo longi. But the researchers identified similarities that may preclude splitting Denisovans into different species.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"This unique combination of morphological traits, distinct from H. erectus, modern humans and Neanderthal-lineage hominins, supports the assignment of most members of East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo as Denisovans," they wrote in the study. This means that Denisovans may have been one human lineage that adapted to diverse ecological zones across Asia over hundreds of thousands of years.

"It is still possible that there are some other lineages that existed in East Asia during the time Denisovans are known to have existed," study co-author Qiaomei Fu, director of the Ancient DNA Laboratory at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, told Live Science in an email.

"We know from DNA that Denisovans were a very varied group genetically, which split early into different populations," Chris Stringer, a paleoanthropologist at the Natural History Museum in London who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email. "These could have developed a lot of morphological variation, which may well surprise us as the sample of fossils grows."

The researchers also produced a new reconstruction of what a Denisovan man might have looked like. A previous DNA study suggested that Denisovans likely had dark skin, brown hair and brown eyes. The new reconstruction shows the Denisovan looking directly at the viewer, with his low, wide braincase mostly obscured by dark hair flowing back from his massive brow ridge. There are clear similarities between the Denisovan man and Neanderthals as well as modern humans, but the Denisovan has a distinct visage all his own.

Xing, S., Wu, Z., Shao, Q., Ge, J., Bennett, E. A., Rao, H., Lin, S., Zhao, Y., Liu, F., Liu, Y., Zhou, K., Feng, X., Jiangzuo, Q., & Fu, Q. (2026). The proteome of Middle Pleistocene Xujiayao and common Denisovan morphology. Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11132-z

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6551. Simple-Is-Best Stuffing

More than a decade after Victoria Granof introduced this classic Thanksgiving stuffing recipe, it remains a staff and fan favorite. As former test kitchen director Carla Lalli Music puts it, it’s “everything you want about stuffing—straight down the middle.”

The recipe earns its name: buttery bread, sautéed onions and celery, and plenty of fresh herbs, with no unnecessary extras. Irregular, torn pieces of crusty bread create craggy edges that turn golden and crisp, while the broth-and-egg mixture renders the tender, custardy middle. Fresh parsley, sage, rosemary, and thyme (sing it with us) bring familiar holiday flavor, backed by a generous amount of butter.

Homemade turkey stock is welcome, but good low-sodium chicken broth from a carton works well. (Or use vegetable broth to make this stuffing vegetarian.) Get the first bake out of the way a day ahead, saving the browning for just before dinner.

Pair it with the rest of our classic Thanksgiving menu →

Choose a sturdy, crusty loaf, such as pane Pugliese, a French white boule, or a country-style sourdough. Skip soft sandwich bread, which can turn mushy once the broth goes in. Weigh out 1 lb. before drying it—the 10-cup measurement is approximate—and don’t skip drying the torn bread in a low oven, even if your loaf is already a day old.

Why bake the stuffing covered, then uncovered?

The covered bake cooks the stuffing through while retaining moisture; the uncovered bake gives you a crisp, golden top. The interior should be tender and cohesive, not dried out. Keep an eye on the stuffing during the second bake rather than assuming it needs the full time. The finished stuffing should be golden and crisp on top and reach 165°F in the center.

Yes. Bake it covered up to three days ahead, until the center reaches 165°F, then let cool briefly and refrigerate within 2 hours. Save the uncovered browning step for serving day. Return the stuffing to a 350°F oven, uncovered, until crisp on top and 165°F in the center, about 45–60 minutes. For longer-term prep, follow our guide to making and freezing stuffing ahead.

What’s the difference between stuffing and dressing?

Stuffing usually refers to a mixture cooked inside a turkey, while dressing is baked separately—but plenty of cooks use the names interchangeably. We prefer versions cooked outside the turkey for the crisp top and edges, but feel free to call it whichever name you grew up using.

Looking for a different take? Try our Sausage-and-Herb Stuffing, Cornbread Dressing With Sausage and Corn Nuts, or any of our other favorite homemade stuffing recipes.

Preheat oven to 250°. Grease a 13x9x2" baking dish with unsalted butter and set aside. Scatter 1 lb. good-quality day-old white bread, torn into 1" pieces (about 10 cups), in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet. Bake, stirring occasionally, until dried out, about 1 hour. Let cool; transfer to a very large bowl.

Meanwhile, melt ¾ cup unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat; add 2½ cups chopped yellow onions and 1½ cups ¼" slices celery to melted butter. Stir often until just beginning to brown, about 10 minutes. Add to bowl with dried bread; stir in ½ cup chopped flat-leaf parsley, 2 Tbsp. chopped fresh sage, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh rosemary, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh thyme, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. freshly ground black pepper. Drizzle in 1¼ cups low-sodium chicken broth and toss gently. Let cool.

Preheat oven to 350°. Whisk 2 large eggs and remaining 1¼ cups low-sodium chicken broth in a small bowl. Add to bread mixture; fold gently until thoroughly combined. Transfer to prepared dish, cover with foil, and bake until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center of dressing registers 160°, 35–40 minutes.

Uncover dressing; continue to bake until set and top is golden brown and crisp, 35–45 minutes longer.

Do ahead: Dressing can be baked (before browning) 1 day ahead; uncover and let cool, then cover and chill. Uncover and bake until top is golden brown and crisp, 45–60 minutes.

Leftover stuffing? Use it up in our Winter Panzanella With Stuffing Croutons →

Editor’s note: We first published this Thanksgiving stuffing recipe in our November 2012 issue as ‘Simple Is Best Dressing’; it has been updated for style. Head this way for more of our favorite Thanksgiving dinner side dishes→

#6550. I Went To Bermuda & Fell In Love With The Dark ‘N’ Stormy

You know an island is really fun when it has a national cocktail. Before heading to Bermuda, I didn’t even realize its national drink was the Dark ‘n’ Stormy. I should have, given its deep roots and ties to rum, especially Gosling Rum. And even though I knew what the drink was, I had never had one. I was excited to try my first one right where it was created!

Long story short: I was not disappointed. The Dark ‘n’ Stormy isn’t too sweet, has a strong ginger kick, and, best of all, is easy to make at home. I also love a layered drink. Even one that looks like an eerie cloud is so pretty to look at. I think this drink finally turned me into a rum lover.

When I normally think of a rum drink, I think of all the fun, tropical ones, like a piña colada or strawberry daiquiri. Perfect for sipping on the beach or by the pool.

But the Dark ‘n’ Stormy is made for the fall and winter. It’s spicy from the ginger beer, which pairs so well with the sweet molasses flavor of the dark rum. Get the spiciest ginger beer you can get your hands on. The more ginger flavor, the better, I think. A chilly fall night deserves this drink. If there's a thunderstorm, major bonus points.

Bermudians are natural storytellers, and after hearing any of their stories, you’d be hard-pressed not to try their favorite drink. Legend has it that after being served this drink, a sailor thought it looked like the worst kind of cloud, one only a fool or a dead man would sail under. It makes you shudder to order one, but it’s too good to stop you.

You need two ingredients to make a Dark ‘n’ Stormy. Gosling Rum and ginger beer. It is common to add a squeeze of lime, which is always a good idea. I don't find it totally necessary because I like keeping it on the warm, darker side. The simple, straightforward version is incredible as is. If you have a lime on hand, then go for it. Don’t go out of your way to buy some limes, though.

I had one riff on the classic that was worth the extra ingredients, though. When we stopped into the Rosedon Hotel, they made us one that included burnt honey, cardamom, and orange zest. It was so delicious, and I could have had multiple.

A true Dark ‘n’ Stormy must be made with Gosling Rum. It’s officially trademarked by them, and it’s hard to argue with the original recipe. If you are going to make one, it’s worth getting the correct ingredients, especially when there are so few.

To make the rum floater stay on top, pour the rum in slowly. As with most layered drinks, the balancing act is delicate. A lot of ice helps, too. If you pour slowly, the rum will stay toward the top. I like to give it a gentle stir before I start drinking, without fully combining the two. I like getting drinks of pure ginger beer every once in a while.

Find your perfect rum-to-ginger-beer ratio. Dark ‘n’ Stormies are often 2-to-1 ginger beer to rum. If you like yours stronger, add a bit more rum. It all depends on how “stormy” you want your drink. When you make drinks at home, you are the bartender and can find your perfect ratio.

Now, if only I could sip on one of these back in Bermuda. That would be ideal. I wouldn’t even mind if it was during a storm.

#6549. 16 Excellent Restaurants to Try in Nashville

Nashville has long been a haven for aspiring country stars and songwriters, but these days, my hometown is also experiencing a surge in culinary talent. A decade or two ago, finding hand rolls made with fish from Tokyo or natural wine by the glass was a challenge. Now, we’re in business, with more options coming down the pike at a rapid pace.

Born and raised in Nashville, I spent my childhood digging into plates of fried chicken with sides of squash casserole and turnip greens at Elliston Place Soda Shop and meandering out to Highway 100 for a plate of biscuits at The Loveless Cafe—establishments that have fed this city for generations. We’ve always eaten well here, but as the city has changed, so have its tastes, expanding beyond the down-home cooking visitors might expect.

That’s a good thing. Ours is a vibrant dining scene that caters to all tastes and budgets, from experimental fine dining to tried-and-true lunch counters. Use this as your primer to getting a taste of Music City. Whether you’re craving a plate of hot chicken from Prince’s or a piece of freshly butchered bluefin tuna, Nashville has it.

Tucked into an alley attached to the Nashville Arcade lies one of Nashville’s dreamiest new bars, an oasis of blush Italian marble and cocktails that defy convention. The product of chef Julia Jaksic and beverage director Owen Gibler, it offers downtown a much-needed respite from honky-tonks and domestic beers. Gibler uses digestifs and aperitifs to create cocktails that have exceptionally aromatic qualities on the nose and on the palate. Jaksic’s menu of bites is designed to accompany cocktails and conversation. Think gorgeous little snacks like cheesy gougères with spicy ’nduja and fluffy focaccia topped with rich stracciatella and mortadella. The bar has quickly amassed a crowd of regulars and industry pros. Come for the drinks, stay for the impeccable vibes and tunes on an analog reel-to-reel tape player.

Visiting Nashville? Step one: Book your reservation at Kase x Noko, the tiny omakase spot that’s connected to uber-popular Noko. Step two: Book everything else on your trip around that reservation. That’s because this 14-seat sushi counter is one of the hottest tickets in town, offering a 14-course omakase at an unheard of $75 price point. There are ways to ratchet up the bill, of course, with add-ons like “steak and eggs”—nigiri stacked with A5 Wagyu, uni, and caviar—or flame-seared yellowtail belly, expertly formed and presented by chef and co-owner Dung “Junior” Vo and his crew. The playlist is curated by partners Wilson Brannock and Jon Murray, leaning heavily on early-2000s hits, an excellent background for cocktails starring flavors such as shiso, yuzu, and pandan.

What started as a pandemic-era tortilla pop-up quickly blossomed into a very popular food truck, followed by a tortillería, and now a full-service restaurant in the Gulch, serving chef Julio Hernandez’s Tennessee-Mexican dishes. Hernandez, who grew up among Tlaxcala’s corn and cooked his way through New York and Nashville kitchens, serves dishes such as grilled chorizo with heirloom beans, served with collard greens with smoked ham hock, salsa verde, and tortillas, and Tennessee trout with popcorn grits. The heart of it all is the masa that’s nixtamalized in-house using corn from Mexico and, more recently, Tennessee farms. Mezcal and tequila cocktails are thoughtful and plentiful.

Turkey and the Wolf was born in New Orleans, where it became an instant hit for its irreverent vibes and gonzo takes on Southern favorites. Luckily for Nashville, chef-owners Mason Hereford and Lauren Agudo were lured here by its friendly restaurant community, and they teamed up with chef-partner Will Mondros to open the Icehouse in a cinder-block building and covered patio on a scruffy corner lot in East Nashville that was once a dog park. Now, the yard is filled with thrifted tables, an Airstream that serves as the office, and sculptures including a brontosaurus and a life-size rearing horse. The menu includes hits that helped launch Turkey and the Wolf to fame, like the collard melt oozing with slow-cooked greens, Swiss cheese, and Russian dressing, and the towering bologna sandwich stacked with thick slices of fried bologna and a healthy handful of vinegar potato chips. But the Icehouse has its own personality and surprises, including a buttery, flaky roti full of juicy lamb and topped with handfuls of herbs. Specials are constant and often experimental, the beers and cocktails are ice-cold, as the name implies, and there’s often live music in the yard. There’s always a party going on at the Icehouse.

Even if you read the directions closely—“follow the red light”—it may still take you a moment to find the entrance to 888, the Japanese listening room located below the towering JW Marriott, just around the corner from the main hotel entrance. Once inside, the vibes are groovy and the fish is fresh. In fact, diners visiting on the second Saturday of the month will witness master sushi chef Kiichi Okabe breaking down an enormous bluefin tuna, which is then served for immediate, luxurious consumption. Beyond Okabe’s sushi menu, try larger plates like a koji-marinated rib eye cooked over binchōtan charcoal, or the donabe with chicken thighs, mushrooms, and cured egg yolk. The restaurant is styled after a kissa, a Japanese vinyl listening room, and it delivers heavily on that promise with rotating DJs who play soul, funk, disco, and more, as well as full album parties that require silence from the room. Don’t miss out on the Silken Spirit Martini, a tableside service that includes the use of a hand-cranked mechanical shaker to mix Japanese vodka or gin with sake and orange bitters.

2105 Elliston Place, Nashville, TN 37203(615) 219-2704

Aside from hot chicken, Nashville’s other hometown food is the meat ’n’ three, a plate lunch consisting of a protein and three sides. The Southern classic is a specialty of Elliston Place Soda Shop. Opened in 1935, it is one of the few remaining (and best examples) of the genre. Generations of Nashvillians have graced the red leather booths and black-and-white-tiled floors over the years, tended to by a staff that feels like it turns over about once a century. (Ms. Linda, “the pie lady,” still makes her beloved coconut meringue pies every morning.) Though Elliston Place moved to a newer space next door a few years ago, it still features the soda counter and pressed-tin ceiling, which makes the milkshakes and sundaes taste like the good old days.

International Market introduced Nashvillians to Thai food in the 1970s, when it opened on Belmont Boulevard serving an exceptionally affordable steam table lunch of Thai and Chinese dishes. Now, with a new location (across the street) and new ownership (Anna and Arnold Myint, children of the original owners), the restaurant incorporates high-quality local meats and produce in an updated setting—though thankfully the original mustard-and-orange bench seating came along for the ride. The kitchen is now a proving ground for chef Arnold Myint, a James Beard semifinalist. Menu items venture beyond the typical selections of curries with five-spice duck lo mein, shrimp and pineapple curry, and red curry rice ball wraps. At lunch, diners can choose from the classic steam table or order from the menu; nighttime brings table service with Singhas and craft cocktails.

At Locust, chef Trevor Moran created his own culinary genre blending influences from Japan to his native Ireland. I’ve eaten briny Belon oysters that tasted—pleasantly—like licking a battery; a roast sole served with morels and uni; and a bowl of tiny sea snails served with toothpicks and spicy salt. The DIY beef tartare hand rolls—freshly ground bottom round, fluffy rice, and smoky pickled egg cream, plus freeze-dried capers and nori for rolling—are a must, as is the tuna crisp, featuring house-cured slices of tuna loin and belly atop a fried wonton crisp slathered with horseradish. The chefs deliver these dishes to the tables themselves to an eclectic soundtrack featuring everything from Meat Loaf to old-school hip-hop. The drink list is heavy on natural wines, though my go-to is the Toki Highball cocktail or a can of sake. In homage to Moran’s birthplace, there’s also Guinness by the pint, and Irish gin and tonics compete with Orion beer and sake cups.

The diminutive Kisser, modeled after a Japanese kissaten, a neighborhood spot serving comfort food where locals can eat, drink, and hang out, has been a smash hit since opening in 2023. After spending years in some of the best kitchens in L.A. and Nashville, co-owner couple Brian Lea and Leina Horii decided to focus on their own vision. Inspired in part by Horii’s family sushi restaurant in California, the menu blends traditional Japanese cuisine and their fine-dining techniques with dishes like onigiri stuffed with snow crab and avocado, a perfectly crispy chicken katsu sandwich on fluffy housemade milk bread, and bowls of udon in delicate broth. It’s one of the best places in town to enjoy fresh fish, particularly the chirashi bowl brimming with pristine sashimi and glistening salmon roe. Make sure to end your meal with a green melon cream soda or a crackly miso crème brûlée.

Folk is a neighborhood gem that Nashville needs now more than ever as hotels and chains threaten to take hold of the dining scene. The restaurant is perched on a quiet corner in East Nashville’s McFerrin Park and welcomes diners with wood-fired sourdough-crust pizzas—my favorite is adorned with littleneck clams, parsley, bonito, and lemon—and rustic Italian-leaning dishes like Marcella beans with spicy pepper relish, bouncy focaccia with whipped ricotta, and more. From the high-ceilinged dining room, adorned with paper lanterns and exposed-brick walls, you can glimpse the bustling kitchen and blazing pizza oven. Natural wines and classic cocktails are the move at the bar, where the afternoon light streams in during the daily apéro hour. The crowd of shockingly healthy houseplants are as well-nourished as the patrons.

Not far from Folk stands a Tex-Mex taco shop with a sense of humor where you can gobble down one chef’s highly agreeable take on Taco Bell’s Crunchwrap. To make it, chef Bryan Lee Weaver (also of Butcher & Bee) fills his fluffy handmade tortillas with Texas red chili, pork green chili, or both when you order it “Xmas-style.” If tacos are more your speed, you’ll find toppings like brisket, tater tots, and freshly roasted Hatch chiles. To me, the sleeper hit is the vegetarian taco with charred poblano, whipped feta, and crispy rice, thanks to its variety of textures and smoky heat. The queso dip comes with more of those warm, velvety tortillas (never chips!), and the frozen margaritas are tart and free of sickly-sweet sour mix. The interior offers retro-diner vibes, with a Formica bar and red leather booths, but there’s nothing like grabbing a patio seat in the summertime to let those margs work their Texas magic.

Lucky for Nashvillians, former Per Se chef and Nashville native Julia Sullivan came home to open her first solo restaurant in Henrietta Red. This airy, tiled Germantown spot boasts an oyster bar glistening with mollusks, including Maine’s salty Mookie Blues and Alabama’s buttery Murder Points. Despite Nashville’s landlocked status (the Cumberland River doesn’t count), Henrietta Red deftly combines coastal ingredients with Southern flavors in dishes like oysters roasted with ‘nduja butter and whole trout with dandelion greens. Wood-fired seafood is the focus here, but the fresh pastas and vegetables—particularly the beet salad with pistachio and mint—stand out too. Brunch brings its own reason to visit, with dishes like shrimp toast with beets and tahini, and smoked fish cakes with lemon-fennel aïoli.

Despite the ever-widening swath of restaurants serving Prince’s signature dish around the globe, you have to visit the original purveyor to get real-deal Nashville hot chicken. As the story goes, the ultra-spicy sandwich was created as punishment by a jilted lover of Thornton Prince; but, instead of catching on fire, Prince loved the spice so much that he’d go on to perfect the recipe that launched his business. Today, Prince’s remains the best in class, serving up fried chicken spiced with cayenne pepper oil atop a slice of white bread with a pickle (a foil to all that cayenne). If you’re sticking closer to downtown, swing by Prince’s outpost in the Assembly Food hall to get your hot chicken fix.

Wood-paneled walls line the dining room of this classic meat ’n’ three restaurant that’s been serving up Southern soul since 1952. Every day, the fourth-generation owners welcome a regular crowd hungry for roast beef, baked ham, and pit barbecue, plus daily specials like fried catfish, chicken and dumplings, and throwback fixins like candied yams, turnip greens, baked apples, fried corn, and creamed potatoes. Wendell Smith’s is a slice of Nashville that has hung on to its corner lot despite unchecked development all around it, still sharing space with the adjacent liquor store of the same name that’s been operating just as long.

What began 70 years ago as a humble motel and café at the start of the Natchez Trace Parkway has been thriving from the moment Lon and Annie Love began serving biscuits and fried chicken to travelers out of their home kitchen. After their continuing success, the couple turned their home into a restaurant and opened 14 rooms as a motel to accompany their new dining destination. The motel went out of operation years ago, and its rooms are now home to retail space, with smoked hams, jams, and biscuit mix on offer. Though there is now expanded outdoor seating and an outdoor bar serving bloody Marys when the wait is long, there’s nothing better than grabbing a seat in the tiny dining room that still feels like home.

An institution since 1974, this legendary West Nashville steakhouse is a windowless dining room featuring backlit stained glass, carpeting, a stone fireplace with a roaring fire (most nights), and sporty portraits of the hounds and horses that once lived on the grounds of the abutting Belle Meade Mansion. Martinis and Manhattans pair perfectly with Sperry’s steaks and seafood, from a filet Oscar smothered in crabmeat and béarnaise to king crab legs served with drawn butter. Nashville’s very first salad bar remains gloriously intact here, and diners can pile their plate with neon-green goddess and bacon crumbles (though the plated iceberg wedge salad topped with bacon and black olives is my choice). Bananas Foster, another highlight, is served tableside in a plume of booze-soaked flames and cinnamon-fueled sparks. The doors open at four for happy hour, when sausage-stuffed mushrooms and discounted cocktails draw a steady stream of locals each day.

Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.

A new study with data from mice and human tissues suggests that, in ulcerative colitis, immune cells in the gut might make pain-sensing nerves hypersensitive.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

People with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) experience gut pain that can be severe, and it doesn't always go away when their inflammation is under control and their colonoscopy looks normal. Now, in a new laboratory study, researchers found a previously unknown pain pathway that may explain this phenomenon.

The findings, published Oct. 23 in the journal Science Immunology, also point to a potential way to block that pain.

"Inflammation in the gut has always been thought of like a fire: the sensory nerves alarm because of the smoke and the heat, and when the fire is put out the alarm should stop," said study co-author Dr. Heng Xu, a physician at Ninth People's Hospital in Shanghai. Xu and his colleagues set out to try to isolate what could be causing the pain even when there's no visible "fire" or "smoke."

"What we found is that the tissue itself changes consistency," Xu told Live Science in an email. "It becomes stiff and less elastic, a bit like a scar, and that stiffness alone keeps triggering the alarm even after the fire is out."

In ulcerative colitis, the most common form of IBD, inflammation causes ulcers in the gut, as well as symptoms like bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramping. Several medications can help quell this inflammation, but that doesn't necessarily eliminate patients' pain. The researchers wondered if immune cells that live in the gut might contribute to that ongoing pain.

They zoomed in on a protein called Piezo1; in immune cells, it's known to play a role in inflammation, and in neurons, it contributes to pain signals. The team looked at whether this protein's activity changed in the context of colitis.

"We started with sequencing data that reads cells one at a time, from the gut tissue of patients with ulcerative colitis and from mice with the disease," Xu said. "One cell type stood out: an immune cell that lives permanently in the gut wall, rather than arriving from the bloodstream when there's trouble." The quantity of these cells was higher in colitis than in healthy guts, and the cells carried more Piezo1 than the other cells analyzed.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"They sit touching the nerve endings," Xu added.

In several experiments with lab mice with colitis, the team used a probe to press on the gut tissue and measure how hard it was. This showed that, compared with healthy mice, the gut was stiffer in two models of disease: one with visible inflammation and another with almost none.

They also measured pain levels in both sets of mice. "In mice with almost no visible gut inflammation, the pain was still there, which is why a colonoscopy can look normal while the patient hurts," Xu said.

They then looked at Piezo1 in both sets of mice. The protein sits in the immune-cell membrane, and when the stiffened tissue around it is pulled or squeezed, it's as if a button were pressed and a channel opens, Xu said. This sets off a chain reaction that leads to pain, Xu said.

That's because calcium ions rush into the cell via the channel, and that surge sends a protein called NF-kB from the cell's interior fluid into its nucleus — the control center where DNA is stored. There, NF-kB plugs into a gene, ordering the cell to manufacture nerve growth factor (NGF) that then exits the immune cell.

This NGF, which is known to amplify pain signals in the body, interacts with nearby pain-sensing neurons. These nerve endings grow denser and become hypersensitive, which makes ordinary gut activity painful, the study suggests.

This newly described mechanism could help explain why ulcerative colitis patients can sometimes contend with pain even when their colonoscopies look normal.

The researchers used chemicals as on-off switches for Piezo1 in immune cells, opening the channel with one and closing it with another. As they did this, they tracked calcium signals and NGF production, and both rose and fell in step with the switch. This result suggests that Piezo1 activity is both necessary for this response and, on its own, enough to trigger it in these cells, Xu said.

Blocking this chain of events abolished the pain hypersensitivity in both sets of mice. The researchers tried completely removing the Piezo1 gene from the gut immune cells and found that this eliminated the pain. Removing the gene also caused no problems in healthy mice, they noted.

The study was "well controlled," said Hongzhen Hu, the scientific director for the Mark Lebwohl Center for Neuroinflammation and Sensation at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, who was not involved in the research. Future research should address the chemical messengers that coordinate inflammation, called cytokines, and determine whether the same chain reaction occurs in human cells, he said in an email.

The mouse experiments also may not reflect long-term, chronic disease in patients, given the mice experienced symptoms only transiently, Xu said.

Xu and his colleagues are now aiming to develop a drug that can target Piezo1 to switch off gut pain locally without suppressing the entire immune system. This would be a more targeted treatment than current options, such as immunosuppressants or opioids.

Other scientists have explored using anti-NGF treatments for other chronic pain conditions but not for ulcerative colitis, Xu noted. Fully blocking NGF might have downsides, he said, since NGF also helps to maintain nerves.

So more work is needed to translate these findings into a treatment. But for now, the work sheds new light on how immune cells can detect a physical change — such as tissue becoming stiff — and convert it to a pain signal.

"For the pain field, that's a conceptual shift," Xu said.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

An autonomous macrophage-nociceptor mechanosensory relay drives chronic visceral pain. Science Immunology, 11(124). https://doi.org/10.1126/sciimmunol.aeb3809

#6546. The Buried Tamales at the Heart of the Yucatán’s Day of the Dead

On a fall afternoon in Halachó, a small town in the Mexican state of Yucatán, Wilson Alonzo stood before a smoldering mound of dirt and began digging. Slowly clearing away branches, leaves, and soil, the chef unearthed a large disc enclosed in banana leaves. He peeled the wrapping back and examined the golden edges of the round tamale inside. He nodded. It was ready for the altar.

Every October and November, Yucatecans like Alonzo gather at the edges of underground ovens and cook mukbil pollo (“buried chicken”), a sacred tamale made only for the Yucatán Peninsula’s Day of the Dead. Known as Janal Pixán (“Food for the Souls” in Yucatec Maya) or Los Finados, the holiday welcomes returning spirits: children on October 31, adults on November 1, and all spirits on November 2, followed by a farewell feast eight—or in some cases, 30—days later. Above anything else that might grace an ofrenda, which could include anything from hot chocolate to relleno negro to beer, mukbil pollo is the star that occupies every altar’s center.

“It is the absolute highlight of the offering,” Alonzo said. One bite confirms why: The crispy, caramelized crust of lard-enriched masa gives way to a smoky, savory mouthful of chicken bathed in a brothy crimson sauce of achiote, tomato, sweet and spicy peppers, epazote, onions, and garlic.

But Alonzo—whose restaurant, Ya’axche, specializes in traditional Yucatecan dishes—said it’s not mukbil pollo’s flavor that nourishes spirits; instead of eating it, they consume the tamale through its aroma. And a crucial part of that aroma, he added, comes from the píib. Dating back to the ancient Maya, this underground cooking technique uses wood, stones, and leaves to impart a slightly herbaceous, smoky succulence to dishes like mukbil pollo—also known as pibipollo or pib—and cochinita pibil.“Cooking it in a gas oven simply isn’t the same,” Alonzo said. “You lose the unique aromas and flavors imparted by the earth itself.”Not everyone sees the píib as essential. In cities, where outdoor space is limited, most tamales are baked indoors. When Steffan Igor Ayora-Díaz, a retired anthropologist, was growing up in the city of Valladolid, his mother made mukbil pollo at home, then brought it to a local bakery to cook in an industrial oven. “Nobody said, ‘Oh, it has to be in a píib,’ ” he explained.

Ayora-Díaz now lives in the Yucatán state capital of Mérida, where he said beliefs surrounding Janal Pixán lean more secular. Not only do most eschew the píib, but he and many of his friends no longer build ofrendas, instead celebrating the holiday by gathering with family over a meal. Mukbil pollo is still important, but it plays a role more analogous to turkey on Thanksgiving. “We’re still going to eat it because that’s the food that you eat on these days, but you’re not really thinking of dead people when you’re eating it,” he said.

While purists decry these nontraditional approaches to the holiday, Ayora-Díaz points out that mukbil pollo is a blend of ancient and modern. “It’s a ‘traditional’ dish, but I’m putting ‘traditional’ in quotes because it’s relatively new,” he said. The Maya have been cooking in píibs and eating tamales for millennia, but ingredients like garlic, onions, and lard arrived with the Spanish conquistadors in the 1500s. And, according to Ayora-Díaz, mukbil pollo only started appearing in written records in the 1900s.Janal Pixán, too, is a hybrid of sorts, blending Christian rituals for All Saints’ Day and All Souls’ Day with Maya beliefs surrounding death and ancestor veneration. In Xocén, a small village of largely Yucatec Maya residents about 20 minutes outside Valladolid, honoring the dead can mean not only praying for their souls at Catholic mass but welcoming them into one’s home as guests and offering them the same hospitality as the living.

“We are dealing with spirits who require respect and specific observances, and who actually come to visit us,” Miguel Tun, a Yucatec Maya tour guide, said. “Even the yards look clean during this time. You walk past someone’s house and see that everything is spotless because visitors are coming.”Tun lives in a modern home next to his parents’ palapa in Xocén. The Tuns, like many Yucatec Maya, make their tamales only for the biix, or eighth day of Janal Pixán, when souls are believed to return to purgatory. In Xocén, the local version of mukbil pollo is perfectly suited for this journey. Called chachak waaj (“red tamale” in Yucatec Maya), it’s like a small hand pie.

“The idea is that the souls can easily carry the food with them,” Tun said. “It’s about seeing them off. It’s like when people travel—say, from abroad—to visit, and we give them a gift.”

This gift isn’t just the tamale itself but the time spent creating it. I visited the Tuns to learn how to make chachak waaj from scratch. We began in the morning. After shredding chicken, slow-cooking sauce, mixing manteca (rendered pork lard) into masa, assembling each tamale, and wrapping them in banana leaves, we needed headlamps to navigate the píib in the darkness.

“If you are going to make an offering as part of a spiritual practice, it has to be something into which you have poured your effort, you have sacrificed your time,” he said. “That holds significant meaning within the Maya worldview.”

The hours spent making chachak waaj also provide an opportunity to reminisce about the dead. “It’s a moment where the whole family is together, remembering things while cooking, making preparations, or kneading the dough,” Tun said. “Sometimes the conversation is about what’s happening in the community, but there are moments where someone makes a comment about something the deceased person used to do or say.”

At 9:30 p.m., Tun and his father returned from the backyard píib carrying several trays of tamales. It was time for the final step. The Tuns, several cousins, and an aunt gathered on plastic chairs and tree stumps and started unwrapping. They inspected each crust, making sure it was sufficiently crispy (the ones that weren’t would head back to the píib). As they worked, scattering charred leaves at their feet, they talked about an upcoming dance recital for one of their cousins.Later Tun told me this is, for him, the most important part of Janal Pixán. “Even though a loved one is gone, you demonstrate strength, you show that the family remains united,” he said. “You want that person, when they arrive, to see everyone together, to see that bond. That’s what matters most. I believe that’s the true essence of the Day of the Dead.”

#6545. The 8 Best Outdoor Pizza Ovens That Deliver Delicious Homemade Pies

We tested the Ooni Karu 2, Ninja Artisan, Gozney Tread, and others to find out which models are worth the dough.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Just like tending to the grill and gathering around a firepit are inherently enjoyable, enjoying a fresh, piping-hot pizza is similarly rewarding, and it’s just a bit more special when it’s homemade. Baking a pie in the oven can yield good results, but there’s nothing like the crunchy crust and smoky flavor of a pizza made in a proper hearth. If you’re hoping to replicate your favorite restaurant’s pie, an outdoor pizza oven can take your homemade slices from decent to genuinely artisan.

Stand-alone and countertop outdoor pizza ovens reach much higher temperatures than regular ovens, and in less time. That high heat is exactly what you need for a perfectly cooked pizza crust—and several of the models we tested can cook up a pie in as little as 60 seconds.

Plus, many of the best outdoor pizza ovens we write about are suited for cooking other tasty foods, just like a real hearth. You can make fish, meat, roasted vegetables, and even bread in these wood-fired and gas-fueled models.

To find the best pizza ovens, we looked at models with good features and designs and called in a handful to try out for ourselves. We selected pizza ovens that use a variety of fuels, including gas, charcoal, and wood. Outdoor pizza ovens all pretty much come with a learning curve, but we identified models best suited to beginners and pizza aficionados alike to offer a range that caters to different skill levels.

For testing, we heated each oven for 30 minutes to season them and burn off any oils or contaminants from manufacturing, then let them cool completely. Fifteen minutes after firing up each oven on high using propane burners, we measured the temperatures on the pizza stones with an infrared thermometer.

Then, we made pizza, using the same dough each time, with propane and oak firewood as our fuel. During cooking, we noted how well each oven performed, different features, and its ease of use. Finally—and most enjoyably—we assessed (a.k.a. ate) the pizza. We recommend the following pizza ovens based on our hands-on experience, their specs, and quality.

Over a decade ago, Ooni built its first portable pizza oven with a design that many have mimicked. Our previous pick for the best pizza oven, the Karu 16, has been replaced by the Karu 2 Pro. It’s the exact same as the Karu 16 with three new features: an air vent, Bluetooth-connected thermometer, and an even larger window on the oven door.

Like the Karu 16, the Karu 2 Pro makes 16-inch pizzas fired either with propane or wood. In testing, we liked the locking door with a glass window, which helped maintain a consistent temperature and allowed us to keep an eye on our pizza while it cooked.

Ooni also added a digital thermometer to this model that monitors air temperature in the oven via a wired probe. That info is sent to your phone so you can be in the kitchen prepping more pies or enjoying company instead of babysitting the oven.

Using the propane burner is easy and gets the job done, but we appreciate the large firebox for wood, which provides a lot more flame across the top of the oven. The large capacity also had us refilling it less frequently than smaller wood-fired ovens.

The Karu 2 Pro also doubles as a capable charcoal grill if you want to cook meat or veggies. While we like a dedicated grill for burgers and steaks, the Karu 2 is a do-it-all outdoor kitchen if you have limited outdoor space. The addition of the new air vent even gets it down to a consistent 200 degrees Fahrenheit for low-and-slow cooking.

Full Ooni Karu 2 Multi-Fuel Outdoor Pizza Oven Review

The Ninja Artisan is the only electric outdoor pizza oven we've come across that's worth a double take. It needs to be covered if left outside because of the electrical components, but the body is made of weather-resistant steel.

Our tester, Danny Perez, didn’t have to hassle with pellets or propane to get things started—he simply plugged it in, preheated, and started cooking. It has a max temp of 700 degrees Fahrenheit, which is less than most gas and wood-fired ovens, but it's not necessarily a bad thing.

While a 1,000-degree oven that makes pizza in 90 seconds sounds easy, there's a lot more to it. Shredded mozzarella starts melting in seconds, the dough crust needs a minute to bake, and toppings may require a different cooking time. Electric temperature controls and a lower max heat offer more runway before taking off on your pizza-making journey. Another plus of an electric outdoor pizza oven is even cooking because there's no need to turn the pizza when it's in the oven.

The Ninja has built-in preset pizza modes to cook different styles of 'za: Neapolitan, New York, thin crust, and pan. It preheats to respective target temps for each and then prompts you to add the pizza. Hit start and it starts counting down for a perfectly timed cook.

He tried the thin crust setting, which cooked the pizza at 550 degrees Fahrenheit for four minutes. When the timer went off, out came an evenly cooked pepperoni pizza.

The Neapolitan setting worked great as well. It cooked the pizza at 700 degrees F for two and a half minutes yielding an impressively crisped crust with some leopard spotting.

Full Ninja Artisan Outdoor Pizza Oven Review

A lot of outdoor pizza ovens are portable enough to pick up and move, but they aren't designed with transportation in mind. Fair—most of us park them in the backyard. Gozney put more thought into portability than its competitors with the Tread pizza oven.

It weighs 30 pounds, has two handles on top, and has a manageable square shape. It can go from home to tailgate with ease. We tested the Tread with the collapsible Venture Stand, which gives you a cooking space wherever you take it.

Getting the Tread fired up only takes a few seconds when using the control dial on the side. The flames instantly extended across the roof of the pizza oven, and we wanted things to get hot, so we preheated for about 20 minutes. Once it reached an optimal temperature, we were ready to pitch the first pizza.

The compact size can fit up to 12-inch pies, which is plenty big for personal pizzas. In testing, we found that the oven has great heat retention, so you can cook them one after another. We also found the opening offered enough wiggle room to rotate the pie with a pizza peel for even cooking.

The Tread comes with a built-in thermometer on the side, but we still used an infrared thermometer to measure the temperature of the pizza stone itself. The quick-release gas hose and regulator make for quick setup, too. For those who plan to take the Tread on the go, Gozney also has a handy carrying case.

Full Gozney Tread Portable Outdoor Pizza Oven Review

You'd be hard-pressed to find an electric pizza oven that gets the job done like the original Ooni Volt, but the Ooni Volt 2 is an honorable step up. This model has a smaller carbon footprint than its predecessor, and it's even easier to use.

Messing with temperatures can get complicated quickly, but the Volt 2 has three presets for cooking Neapolitan, New York, and Chicago Deep Dish-style pizzas to perfection. We usually use an infrared thermometer to gauge the temperature of pizza stones, but we trusted the presets and weren't disappointed.

While this electric pizza oven doesn't exactly mimic a wood-fired or propane-fueled model, it has its place in the kitchen. The Volt 2 can be used all year long, is capable of cooking plenty of your favorites, and is much easier to manage. Even if you already have an outdoor model, we'd go so far as to say that you might need this indoor version, too.

Full Ooni Volt 2 Electric Pizza Oven Review

Typically, rotating pizza stones are a gimmick you find on budget pizza ovens to make up for a low temperature range, especially for an electric model. GreenPan’s Stanley Tucci pizza oven, however, has both firepower and a surprisingly effective rotating stone for indoor and outdoor use.

The controls on this model go from 350 to 850 degrees Fahrenheit, so you can use it for more than just cooking pizza. The oven also has a temperature boost feature that allows you to “boost” the top, bottom, or both heating elements. During testing, Ford used this to crisp up the top crust and brown the edges, and this feature offered more flexibility for cooking his pizza exactly how he liked it.

The Stanley Tucci pizza oven uses a round stone, which sometimes can make it harder to accurately pitch your creation onto the stone. With this model, the oven door has a mechanism attached so that when you open it, the stone is lifted and pulled out, making it easier to toss in your pizza and avoid accidental spills and messes.

Overall, this is the best electric rotating pizza oven that Ford has tried yet, though he noted that this design is limited to 12-inch pizzas only.

Full GreenPan Stanley Tucci Pizza Oven Review

The Gozney Dome Gen2 is definitely a luxury pizza oven, but it's chock-full of features that could potentially make it a worthy investment for those who are dedicated to perfecting their pizza and baking crafts.

A 14-inch flue sits atop the roof of the oven, and this was helpful for maintaining airflow and flames. The Dome Gen2 comes with a standard propane burner, and the wood kit is optional. This helps simplify the process for newer pizza-makers, since wood-fired cooking takes some time to master.

One of the highlights we appreciate the most is the size of the oven itself. After preheating, we had no problem cooking two midsize pizzas side-by-side, and we could move the pies around if we needed to slow the cook time.

It takes a little longer for the oven to heat up when using wood, but luckily, changing the fuel mode doesn't make the burner obsolete. We were able to fire up the oven with the burner first, then switched to wood when it reached the right temperature and turned off the propane.

We tested the Dome Gen2 on a somewhat windy day, and the propane burner blew out a few times. To offset this, we kept the temperature a little higher than usual and burned charcoal on the wood tray for better control.

The digital display is a very convenient feature. Instead of using an infrared thermometer, we could monitor levels in real time right on the pizza oven without worrying about accuracy.

Full Gozney Dome Gen2 Dual Fuel Pizza Oven Review

A pizza oven from the smokeless firepit folks? Sign us up. The ease of cooking with a propane burner is tough to beat.

It took us about 20 minutes to heat up the oven using propane, though you should expect a bit more time when it’s relatively cool out and less when it’s hot. In testing, the average cook time was about 90 seconds and required turning the pie every 20 seconds or so.

The Pi Prime’s manual not only had thorough assembly instructions but a lot of helpful notes and tips to get started, including suggested target temperatures for different styles of pizza.

We found that managing oven and stone temperatures didn’t take too much time, although like other ovens without a door, breezy or windy days could make it more challenging. The oven opening on the Pi is 13 inches wide, so 12-inch pies are about as big as this oven can handle.

Similar to Solo Stove fire pits, ventilation holes line the bottom of the pizza oven for plenty of airflow. The Pi Prime is also constructed with durable 304 stainless steel to withstand high temps and different weather conditions.

Full Solo Stove Pi Prime Outdoor Pizza Oven Review

The Arc Lite is about as analog as it gets, equipped with only a pizza stone, ignition knob, and stainless steel insulated housing to bake your favorite pies. While this model is smaller and less features-heavy than the Dome Gen2 we’ve tested, that doesn’t mean it’s any less effective.

It didn’t take long for us to get the Arc Lite up and running. We just connected the hose to the propane tank then pressed and turned the knob to ignite. It took about 20 minutes for the pizza oven to warm up on a cooler spring day, and we maintained an internal temperature of 800 degrees Fahrenheit. The Arc Lite reaches 950, but that high heat requires more attention so you don’t overcook your pie.

The pizza we made was ready in about 90 seconds and had the crunchy crust and bubbly cheese we desired, and the only downside we really came across during testing is that the Arc Lite is limited on size and can only cook up to 12-inch pizzas. Great for everyday bites, but not ideal if you’re looking to host and make multiple pies at once.

Full Gozney Arc Lite Outdoor Pizza Oven Review

Our resident pizza oven expert, Brad Ford, is regularly trying new models to consider for this roundup. In cases where we remove a model we’ve tested in favor of something new, we still like to highlight it here.

The All-Clad Rotating Stone Outdoor Pizza Oven was our previous pick for the best rotating design. It runs on four AA batteries and only requires a push button to start. But for this particular feature, Ford prefers the GreenPan Stanley Tucci Indoor and Outdoor Pizza Oven. It had clear benefits during his testing experience, and the unique lifting mechanism under the round stone made it easier to pitch pizzas into the oven.

Outdoor pizza ovens use gas or wood to create flames across the top that radiate intense heat downward, warming the pizza stone—like preheating an oven in your house. However, unlike your home oven, outdoor pizza ovens can reach up to 950 degrees Fahrenheit.

Once the outdoor pizza oven hits cooking temperature and your pizza is placed inside, it only takes a couple of minutes to cook. The pizza stone or oven floor gets to the same temperature as the roof so the pizza cooks fast and evenly. While it cooks, those flames up top produce a golden crust that’s crispy on the outside and soft and airy on the inside. Because the pizza only takes a minute or so to cook, you can make a few with different toppings one after another.

Wood is the traditional fuel of choice for pizza ovens, favored for the smoky flavor it imparts in the crust and toppings. However, wood (or charcoal) fires take longer to heat up and require more attention to maintain the right temperature. That may not be an issue if you’re only making a couple of pies, but it can become a hassle if you’re cooking multiple pies for a large group, or entertaining a party while you cook.

Propane fuel can heat a pizza oven up rather quickly. Since it only takes around 15 to 20 minutes to preheat, it's hard to deny the convenience of being able to cook a pie in a relatively short time frame. Plus, cleanup is easy when there’s no ashy firebox to empty. Just keep in mind that a propane oven won't give you that unique, wood-fired flavor.

Luckily, you don't have to sacrifice one for the other: A few of the brands we recommend offer extra accessories you can buy to accommodate a different fuel type. There are even some options with combined fuel, so you can heat up your oven fast with the propane and imbue the pizza with wood-fired flavor, too.

The oven’s size determines the maximum temperature output the unit can reach, as well as the size of pie you can cook. Most outdoor pizza ovens are designed for 12- or 14-inch pies. Our Best Overall pick, though, can accommodate pizzas up to 16 inches for oversized, restaurant-like slices.

Pizzas are typically cooked between 450 and 600 degrees Fahrenheit. Classic Neapolitan pizza requires temperatures around 900 degrees—these are the ones with golden crusts, mottled with dark leopard spots. High-end models top out at around 950 degrees Fahrenheit.

The pizza ovens we recommend have max temperatures that far exceed 500 degrees, but note that an oven with a relatively low maximum temperature still gives you a delicious, cooked-through pie—it just may not look quite as picture-perfect.

In short, yes. Outdoor pizza ovens are incredibly versatile. Beyond pies, you can cook meats like steak and chicken, roast veggies, bake bread (like sourdough or focaccia), prep seafood, make cast-iron dishes, and bake desserts. Since it's essentially a super-hot wood-fired oven, you can use plenty of different methods to whip up your favorite foods.

Accessories aren't necessarily a requirement for operating your pizza oven, but they can make the process a lot smoother and safer. We recommend using tools such as a pizza peel to move and adjust your pie, an infrared thermometer to check stone temp accurately, heat-resistant gloves, and a brush or scraper for cleaning the stone.

Outdoor pizza ovens are generally easy to clean and don't require a ton of maintenance since their high temperatures naturally burn off a majority of food residue. Usually, you can just brush off ash and debris after the oven has cooled down. You can also occasionally run it at high heat to get rid of any extra stubborn bits, and wipe down the exterior as needed. Avoid using water or soap on the pizza stone to prevent cracking.
